speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, November 7, consideration of the motion of Ms. Campbell (Vancouver Centre) that Bill C-31, an act to amend the Extradition Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General.

Madam Speaker, when I finished last night I was getting to the merits of the particular bill before the House. Clause 2 of the bill would amend section 9 of the Extradition Act as it is now by adding a new section. Section 9 in its present form provides that superior and county court judges may act as extradition judges. They are not thereby granted jurisdiction to consider habeas corpus matters.
The proposed amendment would say that for the purposes of the Constitution Act, 1982, a superior or county court judge, acting as an extradition judge, would have the confidence as if he were acting as a superior or county court judge with respect to habeas corpus.
Clause 3, the present section requires that an extradition judge send the Minister of Justice a certificate of the warrant of committal. This proposal is to amend the section to increase the 15-day delay for 30 days and replace the advice of a right to apply for habeas corpus by the advice of a right to appeal from the issuance of the warrant committal.
The intent is to cut down on the almost limitless number of appeals, applications for habeas corpus, appeals of orders, appeals of court findings and so on which allowed people like Charles Ng to remain in the country, in his case for six years. Madam Speaker, not being from the west, you may not have known that the estimated cost of keeping Mr. Ng in comfort in our jails, not including his legal fees, was estimated to be $1.5 million.
It is simply preposterous that any government could have waited as long as it has to do something about this problem. I also pointed out that he had a word processor computer in his cell whereas, as I understand it, judges of the superior courts across Canada are not allowed to have computer word processors in their offices unless they pay for them themselves. Only people who are resting in penitentiaries are allowed to have them at taxpayer expense.
There are a number of clauses in the bill which I think are fairly self-explanatory. My time is just about up. I would like to end by pointing out that Bill C-31 is an attempt to streamline the procedure and reduce the delays in the processing of extradition cases.
It cannot be stressed too strongly that the bill does not address most of the 30 items that are being considered by the Department of Justice in its comprehensive review of the law and process of extradition. In other words, it is a short-term band-aid dealing with the most widely known and widely publicized cases, that of Charles Ng, Kindler and some others.
The bill basically would leave intact the two-track judicial executive nature of extradition in Canada. The Fugitive Offenders Act which applies to the removal of fugitives among the 41 Commonwealth countries is not dealt with in any way by the proposed bill.
It is a long way from being perfect. One wonders why the Department of Justice, or more particularly the government, does not have the political will to deal with this subject in a comprehensive rather than a band-aid, relatively isolated manner.

Government Orders
They will have to answer for that to the electorate in the next election. Those of us who are concerned about the general problem of extradition will, I hope, continue to press the government to deal with the subject in a comprehensive manner rather than in the isolated context with which it does here.
The problem has lingered and lingered and lingered. The government has waited and waited and waited. I pay full tribute to the member for Peterborough who along with members on different sides of the House have pursued the government vigorously on this.
I would assume that it is only because of the pressure from people like the member for Peterborough that this basically do nothing until absolutely forced government has finally taken a small part of the bit in its teeth and is trying to deal with an aspect of our general extradition problems in Canada.
When the bill goes to committee, as I hope it will quickly, those of us who have worked in the criminal justice area for many years and who have been concerned about this area will I hope have a chance to do something.
Let me end with a point that was made yesterday. I do not see many people who were here yesterday in the House. A person accused of murder in my province of Alberta about 15 years ago, fled the court process, went to Los Angeles and the trial against the co-accused went ahead. When she was ultimately apprehended in Los Angeles, she was put on the plane the very day or the very day after she was apprehended. She was flown to Vancouver and went back to Alberta where she faced a charge.
There was a delay of what might have been a week, but it was not six years as in the case of Mr. Ng. The situation is simply outrageous. I salute the government for finally doing something about a small part of the problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague on his very capable speech.
He mentioned the work done by the hon. member for Peterborough who, I believe, had a private member's bill before this House in the last session. I believe it died on the Order Paper.
I am wondering if he has had an opportunity to compare this bill introduced by the government with that of the hon. member for Peterborough. Does it accomplish about the same aim? Is the route chosen by the government for proceeding similar to that adopted by the hon. member for Peterborough in his earlier legislation?
That is an excellent question, Madam Speaker, which I would not venture to tiy to answer. I only wish the question had been addressed to the member for Peterborough.
So do 1.1 wish I had thought of it at the time.

Madam Speaker, I am delighted to stand here in this House this morning and speak to the second reading of Bill C-31, an act to amend the Extradition Act.
These amendments to this act have been required for years. Canada has been operating under an antiquated process that started in 1877 and which was modelled after the United Kingdom Act of 1870.
Many of our treaties were entered into originally by Britain in the 19th century with the treaties being applicable to Canada by virtue of her being part of the British Empire. In the new bill is phase one of a two-part update to the Canadian Extradition Act. This bill is the first phase and will streamline a cumbersome and costly process.
For example, two high profile American cases, those of Charles Ng and Joseph Kindler, have been tying up various levels of Canadian courts with appeals for the past six years. I agree, and so do most Canadians agree, with these two persons being sent back to the United States. We must ensure the system is streamlined. It is not fair that our courts be tied up for six years or more. The old law in effect gives foreign fugitives more chances of appeal than Canadian citizens who are charged under the Criminal Code of Canada.
It took six years for these two cases, Ng and Kindler, to be resolved, whereas most criminal matters in our courts are disposed of in approximately one year. Why should Canadians not be afforded at least as many opportunities as Americans and other fugitives in our courts?
Unless we streamline the extradition process, will we not be obliged to change the rules under the Criminal
November 8, 1991

Code so that Canadians can have a more lengthy appeal process? Why should Canada be a safe haven for killers? This is in fact what it is if we do not curb the trend which we have seen with Ng and Kindler. If fugitives and criminals feel free to flee from crimes committed in their own countries and not have to face the consequences for years, if at all, then of course they are going to flee to Canada. Under this legislation there are eight changes proposed. I will just briefly run through them.
First, at the extradition hearing the judge will now be empowered to hear issues under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Second, following the judge's decision, there will now be a right of appeal to either the provincial or territorial court of appeal.
Third, the Minister of Justice will now be allowed to review the case and decide on the surrender of the person soon after the decision by the extradition judge, even if the judge's decision is under appeal.
Fourth, an appeal on the minister's decision and the extradition judge's decision can be heard now at the same time at the Supreme Court of Canada.
Fifth, these changes will cut down on taking the appeals through all the various court levels to the Supreme Court of Canada. Under the old law there were two separate tracks on the extraditability issue and the surrender issue.
Sixth, the new changes will generally leave only one level of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
Seventh, under the old process there was a possibility of seven different levels, depending upon the decisions. That was very complicated and very time consuming.
Eighth, there are new time constraints on the various levels. For example, a fugitive foreign state will have 30 days after a decision of an extradition judge to file an appeal. A fugitive can commence submissions to the Minister of Justice earlier in the process, but must have concluded the making of them by the 30th day after the decision of the extradition judge, and the Minister of Justice would have 90 days after the extradition judge's decision to review the case and decide on surrender, and this can be extended under special circumstances.
It certainly improves an act that is very old and antiquated. The cost to the Canadian taxpayer for the two prisoners I have mentioned who were in our Cana-
Govemment Orders
dian jails for the past six years was an average of $70,000 a year for each of them. When you look at the court costs and the lawyers fees, they are, I am told, in the area of $1.5 million. Canadian taxpayers cannot be expected to carry these costs of processing out of country fugitives and criminals.
With regard to allegations that extradition of persons to jurisdictions where capital punishment could be the decided punishment, on the whole we have to accept the American justice system to be a fair one. Maybe it does not totally agree with ours and we may not agree with their punishment. Some of their states still have capital punishment, which is the death penalty.
We believe these two people were sent back to a fair justice system and that they should be granted due process in the United States.
In the case of Mr. Ng, he had not even gone to trial before coming to Canada. Witnesses in this case were getting older, memories are fading and some are dying. Both Ng and the victims of the crime deserve the right to a fair trail which could be better provided if the extradition process was made more speedy and more efficient.
We must remember that the victims of the horrendous crimes allegedly perpetrated by Ng, their families and the witnesses also have rights. They have the right, first of all, to see justice served and all human rights must be weighed. There are many kinds of rights, social, political and individual, and each must be weighed against the other and we cannot forget the rights of the victims.
We must recognize that there will be instances of imperfections within every justice system, in the United States, in Canada and in other jurisdictions with which we deal. It does not mean to say that the system over all is unjust, but once we recognize imperfection in a system which is just over all, we can attempt to ensure that extra caution be taken in the interest of protecting the individual's rights.
We must ensure that those areas of appeal which have been outlined in this bill will provide protection in cases where there are reasonable doubts. Further, appeals can be made to other jurisdictions, both in the country to which we are extraditing the fugitive and to the various international bodies, such as the UN human rights committee.

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
These other avenues must be utilized so that Canadian taxpayers do not have to shoulder the financial burden alone. One way that we can ensure a more fair Canadian extradition process is to use care when negotiating treaties with countries with questionable human rights records.
Canada currently has extradition treaties with 45 countries. We are in the process of negotiating more. For instance, currently we are negotiating a treaty with Brazil.
If I could interject at this point, there are two young Canadians who have been sitting in a Brazilian jail since 1989. Their greatest crime has been a humanitarian crime. Both of these young Canadians throughout then-lives have been interested and have been working with people who are underprivileged, who are less fortunate than they are. They both come from well-known families in British Columbia. These two Canadians sitting in a Brazilian jail should be brought back to Canada. I feel that our Canadian system is failing those two people at this time.
It is one thing to send someone to justice in the United States, but it it is quite another to send someone to Brazil in order to receive justice. However, we must remember this works both ways and we want to get back any Canadians from places like Brazil.
In principle, I support this legislation, phase one of a two-part update to the Canadian Extradition Act, being sent to committee. I am sure the committee will look at it, hear witnesses and amend this bill to the satisfaction of all Canadians.
I am very delighted to speak in this House on this bill. Many people have approached me from the riding of Nepean, which is part of this federal district of Ottawa Carleton, with great concern that our system has failed them, especially in the case of Mr. Ng and Mr. Kindler.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to speak on this bill. I see in the House the hon. member for Peterborough who has done a great deal of work on this question. I want to congratulate him. I think he is largely responsible for prompting the government to bring forward this legislation as quickly as it has. That, along with the two very well known cases concerning the
extradition of Charles Ng and Joseph Kindler, has prompted this legislation. I do not want to lump the hon. member with those two infamous individuals other than to say that they are really the catalysts for getting this legislation through. The hon. member has done a great deal of work.
This is basically a good bill. This is a question that has been concerning the Canadian public for a considerable period of time. Joseph Kindler committed a murder in 1983 in Pennsylvania. He had been in Canada for six years as had Charles Ng who committed a murder I think in 1985 and fled to Canada. These two men have really exhausted every conceivable avenue in Canadian law to the extent that people really were forced to focus on the extradition proceedings and the extradition rights in Canada. Canadians wanted to know why these two people were able to spend so much time in Canada. Why are we paying their room and board for alleged offences that they had committed in the United States?
It became very ludicrous when we had a free trade agreement. We entered into a free trade agreement with the United States as a close neighbour. We were prepared to have our whole economic future dependent upon the whims of the American government. It turned out a little misbegotten but nevertheless this is what we decided to do. Yet we were not prepared to trust the American system of justice to the extent that we would allow extradition of men such as these two back to the United States to be treated in accordance with American law.
Regardless of whether we like the death penalty or not, the United States has a very high degree of law. Certainly it is one of the foremost countries in the world in jurisprudence and rights of the individual. I do not think we were sending these two men back to a country that would immediately ignore any right they may have.
When the Supreme Court brought down its decision in October regarding both of these men, a lot of people in Canada were relieved that our Charter of Rights and Freedoms actually was able to cope with this. Within the Charter of Rights and Freedoms we were able to say as a country through our Supreme Court that these two men had been treated as well as they possibly could be. Then-rights are not being infringed upon by being extradited to the United States.
November 8, 1991

We have an extradition agreement with the United States. That is the irony. We trust the United States and it trusts us to treat cross-border refugees in a very responsible manner. Yet we were keeping these two men for six years. They were going from one appeal to the other at a great deal of public cost. It is not that we look at public cost in the proper implementation of justice. We do not and we cannot as a civilized country and as a country whose justice system is one of the finest in the world and we like to think is still evolving.
Nevertheless we did feel that there was something here that could be streamlined and could be made more effective.
I would just like to relate some of the new changes to this process that have been brought forward by this legislation. At an extradition hearing the judge will now be empowered to hear issues under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Following the judge's decision, there will now be a right of appeal to either the provincial or territorial court of appeal. The Minister of Justice will now be allowed to review a case and decide on the surrender of a person soon after the decision by the extradition judge even if the judge's decision is under appeal. An appeal on the minister's decision and the extradition judge's decision can be heard now at the same time at the Supreme Court of Canada, which is a very important change. This is going to do a great deal to expedite the decision on extradition matters.
These changes will cut down on taking appeals through all the various court levels to the Supreme Court of Canada. Under the old law there were two separate tracks on the extradition issue and the surrender issue.
The new changes will generally leave only one level of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. Under the old process there was a possibility of seven different levels depending on the decisions. This very much complicated the matter and of course, as I have already mentioned, this was very time consuming.
These are very important changes. I do not think everything that we would have liked to see is in this bill. There are some matters that have yet to be considered. Still it is a step forward. I think it is very helpful.
Government Orders
I would ask the government why it has taken so long to bring this forward. What we see in this legislation is not inventing a new rocket. It is not discrediting the theory of relativity. It is merely streamlining the extradition process. This is something that members of this House have been calling for, for some time. As has been stated earlier, members have actually put forward suggestions as to how this extradition process could be changed.
I feel frankly there is a dry rot in the Department of Justice that has really got to be looked at and it is right in the minister's office. This was once one of the main departments in government. I know that there are a great many capable people in the Department of Justice. Why is it taking so long to get these matters changed?
In January 1990 the former Minister of Justice and present Solicitor General assured us in a speech which I think was in the United States that the department was working on extradition. It was said that this process was being worked on and that there would be legislation coming forward in a short period of time. Now a year and a half later we finally get this legislation. It was I think because of the work of the hon. member that I mentioned earlier that we finally got this legislation. These cases were causing the Canadian public to be absolutely revolted by the way our system was being abused. It is very unfortunate.
What is happening is that our justice system is not leading the country. It is following Canadians and at a great distance. We are seeing that not only in extradition but in cases of criminal violence in Canada that the rate of violence and violent crimes are increasing. Canadians are more and more concerned about walking the streets of this country. They are more and more concerned about their safety and the safety of their families.
We are not getting the response from the minister and the department that we should be getting. This is vital. If we are going to have the Canada that Canadians want and we in this House of Commons want to work toward, we have to have more co-operation from the Department of Justice. The Department of Justice has to realize where things are going wrong and do something about them before we are embarrassed before the world and particularly our neighbour to the south with our

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
outmoded laws. Such was the case with the extradition treaty and the extradition laws in Canada.
I find it really unacceptable. I find it tragic that we are falling further and further behind every year in our need to update the laws of this country and to have relevant changes to these laws. We need to be able to say to Canadians that we are on top of the situation and not give them the feeling, as I fear we do, that we do not know what to do about increased crime and the legal difficulties that exist.
The minister was asked yesterday in the House about the fact that over 50,000 cases were thrown out of court because of the Askov case. That is the case where it was decided that the defendant had been waiting too long to have the case heard. It was felt that this was an infringement of his rights and the judge threw out the case. This has had really incredible ramifications right across this country. As was stated yesterday by my friend from Scarborough, over 50,000 cases have now been thrown out of courts in this country. That is incredible.
It is demoralizing for law enforcement.

Exactly. That is absolutely incredible. One that really sticks in my mind is the case of a young offender earlier this year. Six young offenders had gang raped a 14-year old girl in 1986. They waited for two years to get to court because of the transfer provisions. The prosecutor decided that he or she wanted to have the case transferred to an adult court. The defendants appealed that transfer and then there was another appeal. Finally it was decided that the appeals would be disallowed and the cases had to be heard before a youth court. That was almost two years later. It was two years after the actual process started and more than two years after the crime. Finally the Ontario Court of Appeal said: "That is just too long. The rights of these six people were infringed by this long wait". Imagine.
And they got off?

They got off because it was felt that this was too long. Now that is absolutely incredible. How, in this country, can we have respect for our judicial
system if we are going to have that kind of a result? It is a disgrace. It is an absolute disgrace.
We have to know when a judge is going to resign or, unfortunately, passes away unexpectedly. We cannot let these long periods of time go by without appointing a substitute. I say that with all respect to the government in one area. If there is one thing the government has done right, it is its judicial appointments. I think its judicial appointments have been good ones. I congratulate it for that. Sometimes the cement in this country is our judicial system. That is very important.
I do not want for a minute to minimize the importance of having sound judges on our benches in this country. It is absolutely vital. I know it takes a lot of thought and a lot of consultation. We have the screening committees that are now in all provinces and consultation goes on with the provinces and it is all working.
But please could it just happen a little more quickly? It is estimated now that there will be over 100,000 cases thrown out of Canadian courts within a short period of time. Imagine. This is horrendous. As the justice critic I have had people calling me and crying on the phone. One person in particular will stay with me for the rest of my life. There was a young person who was killed by a drunk driver who is now free because it took too long to bring that case to court. The parents have not only lost a young life they valued and loved dearly but the person who committed this offence is now free. I just cannot say enough about the tragedy going on this country because of the weakening of our criminal justice system.
While I find that this bill is a major step forward, as is gun control, there is an awful lot that needs to be done.
The Young Offenders Act is awful. We are allowing crime to run rampant. We are making little steps forward but crime is making big steps forward. We are falling further and further behind.
I say to the government and particularly the Minister of Justice: For heaven's sake, stop chasing the mice and start dealing with the elephants. Do something quickly. Put a little more time in it and show a little more oomph.

November 8, 1991

Go on the offensive and deal with the problems that are worrying Canadians.
The economy is worrying Canadians, make no mistake about that. Our constitutional mess is worrying Canadians, make no mistake about that. Also prevalent is a concern about the increased crime rate and safety on the streets of this country.
This is a good bill. I support it without any difficulty at all. For heaven's sake play a little catch-up with the shortcomings of our criminal justice system.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for his commitment this week to all these bills which are attempting to reinforce the justice system of this country.
He has just finished talking about a very serious situation, about the number of cases being dismissed because of the lack of resources given to our judicial system in terms of number of judges and the number of courts that we are short. Obviously it is because of our correctional system. There are some correctional services institutions with two or three to a room. It is just a scandalous state of affairs.
The government does not seem to realize that all of our police forces are becoming demoralized. They are losing their will to enforce the laws of this land. They look around and see that after their investigative work, after they have tried to bring the system to order, 50,000 cases are thrown out the window. They say: "As a police officer, what incentive is there for me to do my job?"
Does he not feel that this lack of political will on the government's part, because it is a lack of political will to reinforce the judicial system of this country, is in fact weakening the ability of all of our police forces across Canada to properly do their job?

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood who is a very thoughtful member of Parliament.
We have talked about this particular question. I know the concern he has, being a Toronto member of Parliament, with the problem of crime. I am glad he asked that question because it is an aspect that I did not cover and I would like to because I have had the opportunity to talk to law enforcement officers.
The Askov case and other cases that police spend a lot of time on are being thrown out. Not everyone agrees
Government Orders
with everything they do but our police forces in this country are second to none anywhere in the world.
In other countries caring has gone out of policing. This is not the case in Canada. There have been examples recently of cases where they show concern for the law and concern for the individual. It is absolutely devastating for them to work on a case.
In the case of a hit and run driver who killed a teenager and is now out on the streets, it is the police who have to go to the family and tell them that their child has been killed by a drunken driver. It is the police who get that initial response of disbelief and absolute, complete physical and mental collapse.
It is not a nice job but it is a job they do. They see this and then follow through, they track down who did it and they want justice done. They want in some small way to ease the pain of the people who suffered the loss, to painstakingly build the case and go to court. Then they lose it, not because the Crown prosecutor did not apply the law properly or did not do his or her homework or because of some technicality but because the court decided that the defendant's rights had been infringed because he or she had been kept waiting so long and it should be thrown out.
Can you imagine what that does to the police officer and the commitment of that police officer? That police officer walks out of that court completely dejected. The fact that he or she can then pick himself or herself up to go back and do the job they are doing on the streets of this country not only tells you a lot about our police forces but tells you about the will, determination and commitment of police officers in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, rather than deal with specific cases, as some of my colleagues have done in their speeches, I wanted to turn briefly to the process that applies in extradition cases. It appears there is a great deal of confusion on the part of the public and I think on the part of some members of the House about how extradition hearings work.
It is important to examine the proposals the government has put forward with a view to amending this area of the law. Frankly I think they are somewhat unimaginative, although I agree that they will have the effect of streamlining the provisions of the law. We support them in principle for that reason.

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
The government might have been a little more imaginative had it chosen to give up some of its power. However it apparently decided that was not necessary and it would keep all its existing powers and simply streamline the process to ensure that extradition appeals are dealt with more quickly.
In any extradition case under the current arrangements, the country that wishes to have a person extradited to that country applies before a judge in Canada to determine whether the person should be extradited under the law. The law is in part the extradition treaty that exists between the countries. It must be determined whether the offence is one that is extraditable under the treaty.
The judge makes a decision on that issue. As is the case with almost every judicial decision, that decision is subject to appeal. Either the accused person or the foreign government may appeal to the court of appeal of the province in which the hearing was held. There is a further appeal from that decision of the court of appeal of the province to the Supreme Court of Canada. There are in effect two appeals. The last appeal is by leave. It requires the leave of the Supreme Court to proceed in that court with an appeal.
After the determination is made by the courts as to whether the person should be extradited there is then a further application to the minister by the foreign government for surrender of the accused. The minister must decide whether the accused person should be surrendered, even though he is judged by the courts to be extraditable. That is assuming the decision went that way.
The decision of a minister is subject to judicial review. Therefore appeals to the courts may be launched after the minister has made his or her decision.
This extremely cumbersome procedure might have been shortened somewhat had the minister been willing to give up control of the surrender process and leave that matter to the courts to decide. After all, the surrender procedure has been there for a very long time. I am not familiar with the history of the law in this area but I would guess it is one of those areas of royal prerogative which has hung around for years and years and years under extradition treaties.
Maybe it is time to take a look at that aspect of it, but unfortunately the committee is not going to get that privilege. Not having dealt with the issue, the committee cannot change the principle of the bill. I am sure that the committee chairman will hold that one of the principles of the bill is that the existing procedure be retained. There is no major change in it.
We are not going to get a chance to do away with this largely unnecessary step which would have really shortened the procedure considerably had both surrender and extraditability been determined at once in one hearing. Perhaps it is naive of me to suggest such a thing, but I suspect that there are ways and means whereby safeguards could have been imposed in the law so that the courts could deal with that matter instead of having the minister involved in making a decision on this.
Perhaps there is good reason why the minister should keep that power. I do not know. If so, I am surprised the argument was not raised by the minister in her opening speech. I do not recall a discussion on that particular aspect of the law.
What does the government propose? It states in this bill that there will be the extradition hearing and immediately after that hearing, assuming that the judge decides the accused should be extradited, the minister will receive and deal with an application for surrender. There could be an appeal in the court of appeal of the province from both the judge's hearing and from any argument that might be made with respect of the minister's surrender, assuming the surrender is approved by the minister.
Both would be dealt with at the same hearing in the court of appeal. Both would then be appealed together to the Supreme Court of Canada, if an appeal were allowed by that court, and we would thereby avoid this multiplicity of proceedings leading to extended hearings in both the court of first instance, the Court of Appeal, then the Supreme Court of Canada, back into the Court of Appeal after the minister's determination and then back to the Supreme Court of Canada. I guess it would not have gone directly to the Court of Appeal after the minister, but there would have been three court hearings challenging the minister's decision.
November 8, 1991

The member for Peterborough can correct me if my procedure is incorrect. He is well familiar with the route.
I now recall, and perhaps I am able to answer my question, his solution was to abolish one right of appeal. The Court of Appeal in the provinces was side-stepped. If there had been an adjudication that the accused was to be extradited, then there was an appeal directed to the Supreme Court of Canada, or none at all. That is my recollection but I may be wrong. Perhaps he can correct me in a comment as to what his bill contained that was different from this one.
This should streamline in most cases, but if the minister is as slow in making decisions as has often been the case, I suggest that in fact the appeals will not get heard together. The application for surrender may be sat on for so long that the appeal in a court of appeal may be disposed of before the minister gets around to making a decision. Certainly in some cases there have been delays. I agree in others the decisions have been made extremely quickly. I think the member for Peterborough could cite examples of excessive delay on the part of the minister in coming to a decision. As I say, it might have shortened the proceedings significantly had that particular stage been abolished altogether and had the trial judge and the appellate judges thereafter been left to deal with that issue instead of having the minister involved in the process.
The fact that the government has moved on this after so long is something to be commended, but I wish that it had taken steps to ensure that this would have worked in virtually all cases. I am not certain that has been done. Leaving the two processes of adjudication in the courts and then the surrender issue with the minister leaves the risk that there will be a multiplicity of proceedings at least in some cases. All we need is some major case like the Ng case, which the hon. member for Peterborough has raised so often in this House and some of my colleagues have mentioned in great detail. The new law will be brought into what I suggest would be considerable disrepute. In other words, it will have failed to achieve the objective that is the objective of all members of this House and that is to make this process less cumbersome. All the steps are there.
All the cumbersome steps that were in the law before this bill was introduced are still there and they are not going to be changed by this bill. It is simply that they will
Government Orders
be done in a different time sequence. The risks of the claims that were made before are still there, but they will be done together instead of apart which should shorten the proceedings. There is no guarantee that it will do so and there is no guarantee that the two processes will not lead to different results.
I suggest that it is a situation that the government could have avoided had it been a little more imaginative in drafting this particular bill, had it been willing to consider giving up powers that it now has. But we know that this government is extremely reluctant to give up any powers. We see it every day in this House with its unwillingness to bend the rules in a way that allows the opposition additional rights or privileges in the House. We see it in the various bits of legislation it introduces to deregulate various things.
It does not give up its power. It simply gives up certain regulatory rights, but not very many of them. There are very few in fact that are given up. The hon. member for Peterborough knows this as he has been a critic of the government in that regard. He has been critical of its unwillingness to give up control over a host of activities in which Canadians engage. I suggest that he would have probably been pleased had the argument that I advanced been accepted by the government and the government would have been willing to abandon the surrender procedure and allow the courts to adjudicate on that. I suggest that our courts are well equipped to make that decision.
I suggest that if the process is to be expedited as has been suggested by my colleagues, where additional judges are appointed to assist in ensuring that there be fewer delays in the court system, and had the government looked with some imagination at procedural means of changing the process, we might have got even more advances in terms of reduction of time spent on these cases.
There has been a lack of imagination. There has been excessive delay. I regret very much that it has taken so long for the minister to move to bring forward this bill. I realize the government has proclaimed this week to be justice week, law and order week I think it calls it. It does not like to use justice any more. It likes to talk about law and order because that appeals a little more. The government thinks it is a catch word that will appeal to the public.

While some of the initiatives are welcome, after waiting for so many years, it is unfortunate that the government is using the notion that things are in big disarray as the basis for its proceeding. Frankly the sensational cases that make the headlines and make it look as though things are falling apart are not necessarily indicative of the workings of the system because, in many cases, our justice system does work well and does produce results that are entirely in accordance with people's expectations. Needless to say, we do not hear about those. It is like the proceedings in this House. In this House we do not hear about the things that happen that are normal or sensible and that work well. We hear about the unusual occurrences, the sensational occurrences that take a second but generate acres and acres of print in the media and lots of time on television.
This bill, which is one of those more mundane matters, will get very little coverage in terms of the debate in this House, but nevertheless it is important. The changes that are proposed in the law are important and significant. I know that the hon. member for Peterborough in his speech welcomed this bill. I think he welcomes the general thrust of it as we do on this side of the House. We are happy to support it and will continue to do so. I am hoping he is going to make a comment about his own bill.
Mr. Bill Domm (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
for Science): Madam Speaker, a short comment.
I would like to clarify what I consider to be a misconception about the government's bill. The government's bill has eliminated the two-track system. What happens in the government bill, the one we are dealing with in the House now, is that you have your extradition hearing with certain other features of the former two-track system applied to it, i.e. they go from that hearing to the appeal court in the province. At that appeal court in the province is where the minister puts the comments in dealing with her willingness to extradite the person requested. So there is not a two-track system. It very definitely goes from the extradition hearing to the appeal court of the province with leave to appeal to the
Supreme Court of Canada. It does not move over into federal jurisdiction.
The big feature of this bill, which I am sure the hon. member will be glad to hear, is that we have eliminated the two-track system in extradition. We move directly from extradition to the appeal court of the province only. At that appeal court in the province they deal with habeas corpus and any challenges to the charter that are raised. After that decision is made those are the two court appearances. That is it.
The minister has a period of time between the extradition hearing and the appeal hearing in the provincial appeal court to prepare her case and state her intentions.
The third opportunity, not four but three, the third opportunity is given-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have to interrupt the hon. member and recognize him after Question Period as it is eleven o'clock. We will now proceed with members' statements pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Madam Speaker, through the green plan the government commits Canada to stabilizing emissions of carbon dioxide at 1990 levels by the year 2000. Through the environment committee we urged the government to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by at least 20 per cent by the year 2005 as other nations are doing.
At this week's meeting of the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment, the government is apparently preparing to back away from its commitment to stabilize carbon dioxide emissions by the year 2000. If this is true, the government will lose credibility at home and at international negotiations on a global climate conference and convention. Therefore we urge the Minister of the Environment to confirm Canada's modest commitment to stabilization.

November 8, 1991

When will the government recognize the well-known fact that it is in Canada's economic interest to cut carbon dioxide emissions and thus increase energy efficiency?

Madam Speaker, with the release of the constitution proposals, Canada is presently involved in a debate on our future. Canadians must participate in this discussion and fortunately many want to.
In the riding of Ontario, 11 volunteers representing a good cross-section of interest have formed a committee to help citizens of the riding participate. This group called the People's Forum for Constitutional Change has spoken to many interest groups and service clubs over the past month, distributing the proposals as they travelled.
This week at Trafalgar Castle School in Whitby they held the first public meeting at which seven high schools sent participants. Led by a panel of experienced individuals, a good discussion was held by the numerous participants. Students proved they care.
The People's Forum has scheduled four additional meetings, one each in the communities of Claremont, Pickering, Ajax and Whitby. At each meeting there will also be panelists. The People's Forum will also send a questionnaire with my support to seek the views of all the citizens of the riding. When all these steps are complete, the People's Forum will then present a report which will be submitted to the national committee.
I would like to extend my personal congratulations and thank you to the People's Forum of Ontario riding.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, every week people in the Montreal area read in the papers that their economy is sinking further into a slump.
Last Thesday we heard that 189 employees at Philips Electronics Limited would be laid off. Today the Christie Brown Plant in East Montreal is laying off 200 of its 600 workers. We also heard the STRSM will be laying off 78 of its 600 bus drivers next April. A number of maintenance employees will also be laid off. This morning Murray Hill closed down; another 200 jobs lost.
When will the Conservative government do something to end the economic slump for which it is to blame? When will people in the Montreal area be able to read their papers without being discouraged by the news of further lay-offs in Montreal?

Madam Speaker, Toastmasters International is one dynamic international organization that assists hundreds of thousands, in fact millions of Canadians and people in the United States and around the world, to be better communicators. Toastmasters clubs exist all over North America and in some 50 countries now. Last night in our nation's capital we celebrated a great distinguished toastmaster by the name of Jack Gillespie who has become Toastmasters International's president.
Mr. Gillespie comes from Manitoba. He was a truck driver and has excelled to this very high position of international toastmastership. I am sure this House would want to congratulate him and the wonderful opportunities he has to demonstrate the toastmastership to all Canadians and indeed people around the world.

Madam Speaker, it has been a little over a week since the unfortunate mace incident in the House.
Two matters did give rise to it and I think it is an appropriate time to raise them for the public record. The first is the substantial issue of seniors taxation. There was a motion before the House from the hon. member for Winnipeg to change the taxation of seniors. Many of them pay quarterly now and they are subject to penalties and interest. They are being hassled. It is veiy unfair and seniors are very concerned about it.

November 8, 1991
The Toronto Star just reported that this method of taxation is costing seniors $300 million a year.
I call upon the government to change this procedure. I understand that is happening and I ask the government to report to the House when it has made this decision. I welcome that.
Second, many of us thought that the bell was going to be a 15-minute bell. It was about a four or five-minute bell. The question arises, should party Whips be able to cut short a private member's vote. I call upon the House management committee to look into this and report to the House as soon as possible.

Madam Speaker, I think in a day and age when volunteer activity sometimes is diminished or dismissed it is important to recognize organizations that have made an outstanding contribution to public service and voluntary activity.
In my constituency of downtown Toronto, Toronto Rosedale, last week there was the annual meeting of the YMCA of metropolitan Toronto which celebrated 138 years of service to the community.
I would like to note several of the highlights from that outstanding organization. Last year, for instance, 120,000 people participated in YMCA programs all across the greater Toronto area. Programs were delivered in some 366 different locations. There were over 7,000 YMCA volunteers who donated more than 92,000 hours of their time to help serve. Finally, 18,000 people received direct financial support from the association to enable them to benefit from YMCA programs.
Members on all sides will know that for more than a century the YMCA, the YWCA, the YMHA have made an outstanding contribution to all of our communities.

Madam Speaker, last week the government announced that further federal assistance will be provided to northern Ontario in addition to the FEDNOR economic development program. The Canada-Quebec subsidiary agreement also provides certain regions of Quebec with federal funds for economic development projects.
I commend the government for these two programs. However, they place eastern Ontario at a disadvantage as the area does not have similar economic development programs to support and attract businesses and industries.
The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism recently stated in this House, in reply to a question by my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, that the government "is preparing a program which will address eastern Ontario in particular".
Eastern Ontario is suffering from numerous plant closures, lay-offs and high unemployment. Communities like Cornwall, Hawkesbury and Pembroke are facing tough economic times.
I call upon the government to stop delaying and implement an economic development program for eastern Ontario now.

Madam Speaker, what does English speaking Canada want? The answer can be found in the Spicer commission report.
English speaking Canada wants Quebec to stay but not at any price, recognizes Quebec's distinctiveness in terms of language and culture but not in terms of rights and responsibilities, wants a strong national government, not a weak decentralized one, wants a fast and fair settlement of aboriginal concerns, wants to emphasize what we have in common, not our differences, wants an elected Senate, wants a review of official bilingualism
November 8, 1991

and multicultural funding, wants MPs to reflect the wishes of their constituents, but most of all wants jobs, jobs, jobs.

Madam Speaker, having brought small business to its knees in this country, people will be happy to know that the government is sending the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism to the Soviet Union. If your business in Moose Jaw is in trouble, do not worry, because they are going to discuss methods of operation and ways of encouraging further Canadian commercial activity in the Soviet Union.
I am sure they are going to take with them many copies of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business survey of what small business thinks about this government. Members may recall this is the report that said and I quote:
Members in all parts of the country expressed strong concern that
the country is living beyond its means, taxation levels are too high;
there is a lack of political leadership; too much government and
government is unresponsive.
It is not clear at this moment whether the Minister of National Revenue will attend. Members may recall he dismissed that survey as a scam and the results as hogwash.
Madam Speaker, the good news is they are leaving the country. The bad news is that we are not sure it is a one-way ticket.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of the residents of Brandon-Souris, I would like to take this opportunity on the eve of Remembrance Day to applaud publicly the contributions which veterans have made in the past to protect the privileges which we today all too often take for granted.
Canadian veterans have made an immense sacrifice in several wars, but especially in World War I and World War II. In fact, Canadian veterans played such an important role in the great war that they were regarded and feared as the shock troops which were brought into the most important battles.
Without the sacrifices of thousands of brave and selfless Canadian men and women, the democratic privileges which we know today could well have been destroyed. It is important, therefore, that we say thanks now and throughout the year for the contribution which others so willingly made on our behalf.
It is also essential that we today ensure that we are willing to continue to defend those values which those who went before us were prepared to fight and, if necessary, to die for. To do less than that would be to fail those who have in reality passed the torch to us and future generations.

Madam Speaker, Canadian seniors want to know the government's position on payment of income tax in quartely instalments. These payments put an undue burden on our senior citizens, and the government's statements on this issue have been very disconcerting.
A motion was presented by the Liberal member for Winnipeg-St. James to release senior citizens from their obligation to pay income tax in four quarterly instalments. The motion was supported by many members, and all three parties in the House gave their unanimous consent for referring the motion to the finance committee, for consideration. Unfortunately the Bloc Quebecois used the Standing Orders to deny its consent for referral of motion to the finance committee, after which the motion was immediately put to a vote and defeated by the Conservative majority. The Bloc's refusal was outrageous, especially since its subsequently blamed the Conservatives for defeating the motion. What it boils down to, Madam Speaker, is that unfortunately-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but unfortunately his time has expired.

Madam Speaker, in the past couple of days all Canadians have become alarmed at the apparent derailment of our constitutional committee.

November 8, 1991
Oral Questions
All of us in this House can point fingers and identify weaknesses in the process, but at the end of the day if that process fails, we fail; Canada fails.
Next week, as we all know, Parliament is recessed and it will provide an opportunity for all MPs to be in their individual constituencies and will provide an opportunity for all MPs to conduct forums, round table discussions, town and village hall meetings in our own ridings.
We have been doing this in Carleton-Charlotte and will continue that dialogue next week.
We can put the constitutional hearings back on the rails by listening and consulting in our own backyards. If we can all do this, the process will take care of itself.

Madam Speaker, Amnesty International is concerned by reports that the government of Prime Minister Sharif of Pakistan may recommence public hangings with as many as 40 hangings to proceed next week.
This follows three years of no hangings since former Prime Minister Bhutto commuted 2,000 death sentences in 1988.
These new death sentences issue from the special courts for speedy trials instituted following a change of Constitution of Pakistan in August.
According to Amnesty International, these special courts of speedy trial violate international standards of justice by denying the right to public trial, the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty and normal rights of appeal.
I call on the Prime Minister of Canada to use his good offices with the Prime Minister of Pakistan to have these public hangings stayed and these death sentences commuted.

Madam Speaker, the word "historic" is frequently used without justification.
Yet there is no other word to describe the Middle East peace conference in Madrid. For the second time in its 43-year history, representatives of the state of Israel
looked at their Arab neighbours, not through the sight of a rifle but in the eyes in direct bilateral negotiations.
This is indeed an historic development. The position of the Palestinian delegation was surprising. The Palestinians seem to indicate their willingness to accept a transitional phase and the self-government first proposed in the Camp David agreements of 1978. They presumably now accept that a long-term settlement will require a transitional period to build trust.
The attitude of the Syrians stands in stark contrast to the Palestinians. Syria has shown an unwillingness to talk directly with Israel and is not prepared to consider any confidence building measures.
On a visit to Israel several years ago, I asked a member of the Knesset what Canada could do to help in the peace process. "Encourage the moderates", she said. That advice is as good today as it was then.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry, the time has expired.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
This government obviously does not have a clue what it is doing economically. It says that the recession is over, and yet today's figures show that unemployment is on the rise.
There are 178,000 more Canadians looking for jobs today than a year ago. In one month alone, the country has lost 16,000 manufacturing jobs. When will the minister acknowledge that the government's high dollar and GST policies are a disaster for Canada? When will he take steps to put almost 1.5 million unemployed Canadians back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think there is some encouraging news in the employment figures that came out today.
There have been 43,000 new jobs created in the last month, and that is a total of 108,000 new jobs over the last two months. In addition to that, the housing statistics would indicate for the month of October that housing starts commenced at an annualized rate of 202,000.
November 8, 1991

Oral Questions
There is a clear indication that housing starts will be up in 1992 by some 20 per cent over 1991.
I think the other encouraging news is the fact that yesterday the Bank of Canada rate dropped by some 31 basis points which brings the Bank of Canada rate down to 7.73 per cent. That is consistent with the policy objectives that we embarked upon, bringing down inflation, consolidating our fiscal difficulties and bringing down interest rates.
Bringing down interest rates is the key to growth in economic activity.
[Translation)

Madam Speaker, now that the government sees that nearly one and a half million Canadians are unemployed, why won't it admit that its monetary and economic policies are a total failure? Why is the minister not prepared to admit that his high dollar policy and the GST are crushing the Canadian economy? Why does he not change those policies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member knows that the government does not pursue a high interest and a high dollar policy.
What the government is pursuing is an environment to bring interest rates down, bring inflationary pressures down. The inflation on an annualized basis over the last six months has averaged 2.2 per cent. That is bringing prices down. That is creating a more competitive economy.
When we can continue to bring interest rates down and keep them down, that will be the key to economic activity, the creation of jobs and growth right across this country.

Madam Speaker, last week the minister admitted that his government had been pursuing a high dollar policy when he said outside the House: "We are no longer pursuing a high dollar
policy".
I know he was left with the legacy of his predecessor, the million dollar man who, when he was in the ring, knocked down almost a million and a half Canadians.
Will this minister allow these Canadians to be picked up and put back on the job by changing the GST, by abolishing the GST, and by killing once and for all the high dollar policy that cost 16,000 manufacturing jobs this month alone?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member is totally inaccurate when she suggests that this government has pursued a high dollar policy. We are not pursuing an artificially high dollar policy and for her to suggest that we can artificially manipulate downward the value of the dollar is totally and absolutely irresponsible. It would destroy international credibility. It would create market instability, and it would create long-term high interest rates and long-term inflation. Why does she not start acting responsibly?

Madam Speaker, what is totally and absolutely irresponsible is to put your head in the sand when 1.5 million Canadians continue to be unemployed.
Month after month this Minister of Finance has told Canadians that the nation is in recovery and month after month the evidence continues to mount that the nation continues to be in a deep recession. Now 1.5 million are unemployed and unemployment is up again this month. From August until October, unemployment in Canada has increased from 9.8 per cent to 10.3 per cent. That is a negative, troubling trend for any sober, serious and concerned minister of finance.
What is the Minister of Finance going to do to put Canadians back to work? Is he now saying that 1.5 million, a 10 per cent plus level of unemployment, is an acceptable level of losses in the battle against inflation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I indicated earlier, Canadians are going back to work. There were
43,000	full-time jobs created in the month of October and over the last two months 108,000 new jobs were created. I think that is a good record.

November 8, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-St. Barbe - Baie Verte):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, just last month 20,000 Canadians and their families in the goods producing sector were unemployed. Five thousand more in the agricultural sector are unemployed. Sixteen thousand more families are unemployed in construction. Four thousand more in trade are unemployed. One and a half million families are without work. When will this government begin to put Canadians back to work by recognizing there is a problem with this government's high interest rate and high dollar policy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the last two months, 108,000 full-time jobs were found and that is a positive indicator. The hon. member knows that the unemployment rate fell in the month of September from 10.6 to 10.2 per cent. The fact that the 43,000 additional full-time jobs have been created, totalling 108,000 fulltime jobs over the last two months, is an encouraging sign and the hon. member should applaud it rather than criticize it.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
The minister cites the creation of jobs but has the minister spoken to the 18 per cent of the residents of Prince Edward Island who are unemployed and the 18 per cent unemployed in Newfoundland? Has he spoken to those who are every day seeing their industries shut down, and has he spoken to the farmers who are losing their farms? I say to the minister that he should be speaking to Canadians and not just citing graphs and statistics.
The minister has continually said that we are in a recovery period but ordinary working Canadians and those without a job do not see this recovery. Is the minister simply accepting that 1.5 million unemployed is acceptable? Is that this government's goal, to keep double digit unemployment, or is this government prepared to do something about it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker, it is not acceptable. The government is trying to do something about it. In order to do something about it we had to wring out the inflation and inflationary pressures. We had to bring costs down. We had to bring interest rates down. Interest rates are the key to economic recovery.
There has been a substantial decline in interest rates over the last few months. As a matter of fact there was a decrease of 31 basis points yesterday.
We have a prime bank rate that is the lowest in about 14 years. We have inflationary pressures down to the lowest in 20 years. Those are the fundamental components towards the resurgence of the economy. Jobs are being created. We have put together programs to help farmers in their distressful situation because of a trade war. All of these things are being acted upon.
But it is not simply a matter of snapping one's fingers. The fundamentals have to be put in place and that is what we are proceeding with.

Madam Speaker, I would say to the minister that it is the fundamentals like the GST, the trade deal and the high dollar that have created this situation. Those are the fundamentals put in place by this government.

For instance, we saw this morning in the Quebec newspapers that three more companies were announcing lay-offs: Christie Brown, 200 people; Aerocar Murray Hill, 200 people; Cascades, 250. And there are more every day.
In Quebec, more than 600,000 families are living on welfare. A record!
My question to the minister is this: What is this government going to do now, to give all these people jobs? Not tomorrow, but today!

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a matter of getting an economic environment that is conducive to investment and job creation activity. Bringing interest rates and inflationary pressures down are very fundamental.
The other thing that is very fundamental is putting in place some very important structural changes that will allow Canadians to compete in the global market economy.
Yesterday's Toronto Star indicated that with free trade a printing firm in Toronto, taking advantage of free trade and enthusiastically eyeing expansion in Canada and the larger U.S. market, stated that this year would be its best
November 8, 1991

year in 20 years and the firm is increasing its employment from 22 to 200. That was the Toronto Star.
We also know that the president of Chrysler announced the other day that Chrysler is putting on a third shift in its manufacturing of automobiles; Dupont Canada triples its profit; Piper Aircraft chooses Canada; Dupont opens world scale plant; Dow Chemical opens world scale petrochemical plant. All of these things are the product of the free trade deal and of low interest rates and low inflation. They will provide sustainable recovery with price stability. That is our goal.

Madam Speaker, the minister fails to cite the fact that over 300,000 Canadians have lost their jobs, that the trade deal is an important part of that job loss and this government and this minister knows it. Do they change their policy? No. They go ahead, they take a bad deal and they want to make it worse by having the deal with Mexico. This government does not change its policies and does not listen to Canadians.
I want to say to the minister, each time these questions are raised about the unemployed, he cites more statistics, more graphs. I look at the faces of those hardworking Canadians who cannot afford to buy anything because of this government's policies. I want to say to the minister again: Will he take the advice of small business and get rid of the GST? Will he listen to Canadians and bring in a fair tax system so Canadians have some money to purchase something?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member takes issue with me quoting statistics and articles. If it is fair ball for her to quote articles to me which she purports to suggest are anti-free trade, I guess it is fair game for me to talk about those articles which appear in the daily press which encourage and support the issue of free trade.
I repeat, 108,000 new jobs have been created in Canada in the last two months. We are coming out of a recession. The recession has been much deeper than we had expected but with interest rates coming down, with inflationary pressures easing, with an investment climate
Oral Questions
that is positive, we look forward to robust growth in 1992. We are expecting growth to range somewhere in the neighbourhood of 3.2 to 3.5 per cent.
I can only tell the hon. member that unless we get the fundamentals right, unless we are able to compete in a globalized economy, restructure ourselves and adjust so that we can carve out niche markets in an effective way, we are not going to see it turn around. That is the challenge we as government have. That is the challenge that labour has. That is the challenge that business has. That is why we have to work at this in a partnership arrangement and this is precisely what we are doing.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. This morning there were very disturbing news reports that the Yugoslav army has set up missile sites aimed at Croatian cities and is threatening, to use their words, "Croatia with massive casualties and ecological disaster".
The European Economic Community, and Canada joining in, has cancelled some trade promotion and trade agreements. Is it not time, in light of this kind of threat of genocide that was issued this morning, that we go far beyond this kind of modest prudent measure and stand up and say we will not tolerate European countries selling oil to the Yugoslavian army, we will not tolerate a blockade that starves people in Dubrovnik and that we insist the United Nations step in and take the kind of action that will tell the Yugoslavian army and the Serbs that we will not tolerate this kind of action against civilians using rockets and missiles to end their lives?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the situation in Yugoslavia is very serious and very troublesome. We all hope there will be a way of finding some way to negotiate rather than use weapons to deal with this problem.

November 8, 1991
Oral Questions
As the hon. member knows, this morning in Rome the Prime Minister announced a series of measures which Canada will take with respect to trade issues. We will be suspending our general preferential tariff treatment. We will put Yugoslavia on the area control list. We will suspend all trade promotion and trade support measures and we will be working closely with the European community and going to the United Nations where there will be discussions about further sanctions that could be imposed as well.
In addition, because I know of the hon. member's concerns, the Prime Minister announced this morning that an additional $1 million will be made available for humanitarian aid through the Red Cross to assist civilians in Yugoslavia to deal with this terrible situation.

Madam Speaker, in response to the minister, I take no issue with the measures that were offered this morning, but they are too little and too late.
The reports that we have this morning is the kind of threat of massive casualties and ecological disasters, in the words of the army itself.
I want to ask the minister: Does she not think that Canada could be taking a much stronger role in mobilizing a major international relief effort, breaking the blockade and saying veiy clearly to both sides that the fighting must stop and we must end this persecution of innocent civilians for the sake of these objectives? What kind of tough international actions is Canada going to be promoting and issuing this weekend before this kind of disaster takes place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure that my hon. colleague would agree that in fact Canada has played a leadership role. We were one of the first countries to make the call at the UN for initiatives to be undertaken to deal with this terrible situation.
I know that the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs will continue to be vigorously putting forward our view that there must be an end to the conflict in Yugoslavia. There must be a way of negotiating peace and we will undertake whatever measures that we can to help to ensure that this happens.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
Canadian National is selling the profitable line between Truro and Sydney in Nova Scotia, yet those who are interested are being told that to get more detailed information they have to sign a secrecy agreement and pay $500. Canadians own this railroad, yet the government is denying pertinent information to the taxpayers.
Why is the government doing this? What is it hiding? Why cannot the people in Atlantic Canada know the details of this sale and the information? Can it be that this whole sale is really more misguided and more of a fiasco than we first thought?

Madam Speaker, CN is set up as a Crown agency with autonomy of operation and with a mandate to be as commercially viable as possible. It has decided to call tenders for sale of the Sydney-Truro line. I understand that the bids are now in. It will go through the process. When CN has made its decision, it will forward it to the Minister of Transport and we will have a look at it at that time.

Madam Speaker, included in this sale, I might add, are 3,200 acres of land, a lot of it prime real estate. It sounds an awful lot like another Route Canada fiasco.
Why will the government not disclose the pertinent information about this sale to Canadians? Why does the minister not admit that this so-called hands off, arm's length transaction is really just a farce.
Madam Speaker, if the gentleman would like to give to the Minister of Transport the components of the so-called farce, the Minister of Transport will investigate it.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture who announced an $800 million assistance package to Canadian farmers several weeks ago in response to farm rallies calling for $30 an acre.
November 8, 1991

Has he now decided if all seeded acres will be included in the program? Specifically, will forage crops grown on class I, II, III and IV soils, whose prices have been forced down along with grain prices, be included and when will the pay-out be in the farmers' hands?

Madam Speaker, the decision to bring further assistance to the grains and oilseeds industry was not made because of farm rallies. It was made because it was important that the Government of Canada support a very important economic industry in Canada.
I say to my hon. friend the decisions and the recommendations as to how the money would be paid out is being worked through the third line of defence committees which have representatives of producers, farm leadership, and provincial representatives. When they are able to provide me with the advice, I will make a decision on the options or choices they present to me.
I hope to be able to distribute as quickly as possible the amount of money we would have available. As you know, Madam Speaker, when the announcement was made, I make a commitment that the funds would be delivered before spring.

Madam Speaker, can the minister tell us if the government intends to place further estimates before this House before the pay-out can be made, or will we be waiting for the next budget before the pay-out can be made?

As the
hon. member knows, if there arises a need to place estimates, the government will place those estimates.
He knows the difficulty that all governments, not just the Government of Canada, have at this time in finding additional resources. I hope that there can be a pay-out made in the very near future which will be substantial and which will assist the agriculture community in Canada.
Oral Questions TOUR BOAT INDUSTRY

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. It has to do with Canada's tour boat industry.
Business in the tour boat industry is down about 30 per cent this year over last year. There are several reasons for that decline in business, but one of the major reasons is overregulation of the industry by the federal government.
Can the minister give me a commitment that he will conduct an inquiry into all aspects of government regulation in the tour boat industry to see if, without compromising safety, there are any regulations that can be eliminated or adjusted which would have the effect of lowering costs for our tour boat industry in Canada?

Madam Speaker, I would certainly appreciate it if the member would provide me with the source of his statistics. I met recently with a number of people in the tour boat industry. They are all telling me that 1991 has been a booming year for the cruise ship industry.
If the gentleman has any indication as to what precise regulation is hindering that industry, we would certainly be interested in looking into it.

Madam Speaker, my statistics come from the tour boat industry itself. The tour boat industry is a multi-million dollar industry in this country and it is in a state of decline right now. It employs hundreds of seasonal workers, most of whom are students.
If the minister is not interested in meeting with these people, as I suggested, and examining the regulations that are imposed on them, will he reconsider and either meet with those representatives or get in touch with them and tell them why he will not meet with them, and tell them that the present regulations must remain in place even if it means the decline of that very important industry that is hurting?

November 8, 1991
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, obviously the member was not listening to what I just said.
I said that we are prepared to examine any reduction in regulations that could help the industry provided-and this is what we said all along-that we will not jeopardize the safety of the travelling public.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration and concerns a young Romanian couple, Mr and Mrs. Bursucianu. The minister is familiar with their case. Mrs. Bursucianu, her parents' only daughter, is more than eight months pregnant and the department wants to deport her before the birth of her child, due in early December. Her physicians at the Royal Victoria Hospital all agree that to deport her at this time would have a major impact on her health and that she cannot travel in her condition.
