However, all the department has to offer is a promise to send this young woman, who is in the last stages of pregnancy, a nice comfortable RCMP vehicle to drop her off at the U.S. border. I think that is gross.
My question is this: Is the minister prepared to make a humanitarian gesture and, as requested by her physicians, allow this young woman to give birth in December and make a safe recovery?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as the hon. member is no doubt aware from our discussions, each case is examined on its own merits. The hon. member is also aware that the Privacy Act prohibits us from discussing details of specific cases in the House. However, I have been informed that, in the circumstances, the deportation order will be stayed for the time being.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister of immigration and it concerns his annual report to Parliament.
The minister has considerably tightened up the family class by restricting the definition of dependency. My question is a simple one: Why the attack on the family
class? Is the family no longer important to this minister and this government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, hon. members are well aware of this government's concern for families. The immigration levels announced by my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, reflect that concern. The family class has been maintained. We are not withdrawing from our pro-family immigration policy. According to the immigration plan tabled for 1992, we will raise the level to 100,000 families. For the sake of comparison, in 1984, before we came to power, it was 84,000.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
Despite what the minister has told the House this morning, he is well aware of the fact that housing starts in Canada this year are at a seven-year low. In fact they are 100,000 less than some four years ago. Interest rates are falling, but we still have double digit unemployment.
Will the minister finally agree to introduce a 5 per cent down payment for first time home buyers in order to stimulate demand, in order to create jobs without increasing the deficit and without increasing the national debt?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in fairness to the hon. member I think he would recognize that with the decline in interest rates, the projections by CMHC would indicate that there will be an increase of at least 20 per cent in housing starts in 1992.
Obviously the lower interest rates in terms of the prime bank rate, which is now at its lowest level in 13 or 14 years, will provide an incentive for additional home building.
With respect to the member's proposal, the 95 per cent mortgage provided by CMHC, it is a matter that we are looking at very closely. There are some issues that have to be addressed in terms of what sort of restrictions and parameters one may want to contemplate in building around it. I know the hon. member has been a strong supporter of this particular provision and I can assure him that we are actively considering it.
November 8, 1991

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture.
Recently the Canadian Wheat Board in what it calls an experiment announced that it will be shipping some
55.000	bushels of barley through the port of Seattle. This is the first time that the Canadian Wheat Board has ever loaded grain through an American port.
Will the minister advise the Canadian Wheat Board that sales through American ports create uncertainty in the growth, investment and development of our port facilities and threatens thousands of jobs? Will he tell the Canadian Wheat Board and assure the Canadian public that there will be no more sales of this kind?

Quite to the contrary, Madam Speaker. I would say to the Canadian Wheat Board that it has accepted its responsibility to get the most efficient return for producers and to sell every bushel of grain it can on behalf of farmers in Canada.
The strikes that took place in the two ports east and west harmed Canada's integrity internationally in our ability to supply. The wheat board has made a decision to increase the sales opportunities to producers, and I encourage it to do everything that it can to increase those sales opportunities. The wheat board's responsibility is to the producers.

Madam Speaker, Sask Wheat Pool right now has a 34,000-tonne capacity that is empty. The Alberta Wheat Pool has over
32.000	tonnes that are empty and could easily handle this sale. UGG does not have a ship in port at this time. This grain sale will not be following the WGTA subsidy and this sale was done without consultation with the industry.
It is incumbent upon this government to take a stand in order to show that we have a viable and a valuable transportation system in this country, or is the minister hoping that we will next see unit trains hauling grain down to the Mississippi?
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, I know that the New Democratic Party is quite touchy about the strikes that took place in Canada's two very important ports. It cost farmers in Canada over $40 million every week that the port or Vancouver was shut down.
What the Canadian Wheat Board has done is accept its responsibility to deliver as much grain on behalf of the producers, make as many sales on behalf of the producers as it can.
The hon. member talks about lack of support. I would say to the hon. member, if lack of support is indicated, that Mr. Allen from United Grain Growers says: "Although we have terminals in both Thunder Bay and west coast, we have a responsibility to our producers, not our terminals". The UGG supports the move and I am sure every producer in Canada supports the move.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, I direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister.
A few weeks ago the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans announced a $40 million aid package for the Atlantic fishery. Each province was included except Prince Edward Island.
Will the minister accept his responsibility and provide the much needed aid to the groundfishermen of Prince Edward Island?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in considering the need for an Atlantic fisheries aid program, the department of fisheries and the minister have taken into account the relative income needs and the degree of catch failure in the various provinces.
I am sure when the hon. minister is able to return to the House he can assure the hon. member that the needs of the fishermen of Prince Edward Island will be adequately addressed in any way necessary.

November 8, 1991
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, I can inform the hon. minister that there is a catch failure in the groundfisheiy in Prince Edward Island also.
The province of Prince Edward Island has received less than $150,000 of the $584 million aid program announced in 1990 despite the problems in the Island fishery.
Will the minister realize that Prince Edward Island is part of Canada and deserves fisheries aid?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure the hon. member would agree that this government has taken many initiatives which recognize the importance of Prince Edward Island and Islanders not only with respect to the fishery but with respect to many other areas of economic need in that province. We will continue to do so.
When the minister of fisheries has a chance to address the question of the hon. member, I am sure he will satisfactorily convince him that the fishermen of Prince Edward Island and processors alike are being amply treated as they always have been under this government.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture.
For years Canada has taken a hard line in international negotiations with respect to protecting Canada's supply management system, but now we cannot be too sure.
Can the minister explain what he meant when he said recently: "People are going to have to put a little water in their wine"? Is this a way of saying that it is all over for supply management?

Madam Speaker, I am pleased the hon. member has given me an opportunity to answer his question. I was talking-and I can read the quote to him-about the export subsidies that are distorting the international grain trade. I can hand the hon. member a copy of the transcript.
I said that in order to come to an agreement I believe people in this negotiation on export subsidies which distort trade internationally would have to do what negotiations point them to doing in this area, and that is put a little water in the wine.
Yesterday I met with my provincial colleagues. Our support in the supply management field has not wavered. Every province was represented. We will continue to press our point at the GATT as we have for the last two years. Supply management has worked for Canadian producers and Canadian consumers. This government and the rest of the governments in Canada continue to support it.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
I like what I hear him saying, but I ask the minister how come he also said recently that he hopes that we can find a way to protect the supply management system. We have a way now. We want to save the system we have got, not find another one.
We know that the government publicly defends supply management boards but officials are saying off the record-and it is in the press today-that we are not likely going to be able to save them because we are basically the only country that wants to do that. We are the only country that wants them strengthened and clarified.
If that is a possibility-and I do not think the minister can deny that it is a possibility-are officials working on a fail-back position? If not, why not? If they are, what is it?

Madam Speaker, the Liberal Party may be working on a fall-back position on supply management. This government and the other governments and the producers in Canada are working to maintain and strengthen article XI so we can protect the supply management system which this government and producers support.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs and concerns the situation in Croatia.
November 8, 1991

As we know it is deteriorating. The Serbia controlled army is committing war crimes against the people of Croatia. Yugoslavia as such does not exist any more and this is confirmed by a statement of Mr. Mesic, the last president of Yugoslavia.
When is Canada going to see reality and recognize the democratically elected Government of Croatia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs I could say, as I mentioned earlier, that we along with our allies in the European community have undertaken a series of measures which we hope will bring all parties to their senses, end the conflict and get back to serious negotiation at the table in order to bring about peace in that area.
As I mentioned this morning, the Prime Minister has already announced a series of measures, of sanctions dealing with trade issues consistent with what the European community has done. That along with the humanitarian aid which has been additionally announced this morning we hope will increase the pressure and bring all parties to the table to negotiate a peaceful settlement of the disputes.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is as follows.
Does the government not think that if we had recognized the Government of Croatia when it was first elected and wanted to co-operate as a unit in Yugoslavia, we would not have had this deteriorating situation. There was a signal given to the Serbians: let them fight and let them take over Croatia.
I think it is still very important for us to do the proper thing and recognize the Government of Croatia.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canada along with members of the European community, the CSCE and NATO all believe that recognition for those who wish it obviously should be given, but it should be done within a framework of negotiated settlements.
Oral Questions
Obviously that is what we have been pushing for. There has to be negotiation at which the rights of all parties, the minorities and everyone who is involved in the situation, can be protected and human rights will be able to prevail as well. That is the process we are committed to and every effort that we along with the other countries around the world can undertake to bring that about, I can assure my hon. colleague, will be supported by the Prime Minister and this government.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
It is my understanding that External Affairs has received a request from the Government of Ukraine asking that Canada send three observers to monitor the referendum and elections to be held there December 1.
Will the government agree to this request? Will it arrange to send the three requested observers to Ukraine?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Madam Speaker, again on behalf of my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs, yes, the member is correct. I understand that such a request has indeed been made. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is obviously giving this very serious consideration. I am sure upon her return from the NATO summit next week she will be able to address and finalize this matter.

Madam Speaker, I will take that as a provisional yes and would ask, then, whether or not the government would consider requesting of the Government of Ukraine that the Canadian observer team be augmented by one, to allow a technical adviser from Elections Canada to accompany them.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be pleased to take the member's representation and make it known to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am sure that she will get back to the member accordingly.

Oral Questions EXTRADITION

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs.
In December 1989 two Canadians, Christine Lamont and David Spencer, were arrested in Brazil. They were in a house where it was believed a Brazilian businessman was being held hostage. Despite pleas of innocence and doubts about the fairness of the trial and the justice process, they are still in Brazilian jails.
Given that the parents of Christine and David have made every effort to have them returned to Canada, I ask the minister why this government has not commenced the extradition process to have Christine and David returned to this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I know there has been some columns in the newspapers about this particular situation, but as I understand it there was not a transfer of offenders agreement between Canada and Brazil. The department has been endeavouring to negotiate such a treaty with the Brazilian government but there is not one at this time.
I also understand that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has reviewed this case and at this point does not believe that there has been a denial of justice or that there are grounds upon which she could initiate an approach to the Brazilian government. However, I am sure that if there is additional information that can be brought forward she would be prepared to look at that.

Madam Speaker, this is a heartbreaking situation for two young Canadians whose only crime has been a lifetime commitment to helping those less fortunate than themselves.
Given the belief that there has been a possible misuse of justice by Brazilian authorities, on humanitarian grounds and the possibility of human rights violations I again ask this government to give every consideration on behalf of Christine Lamont and David Spencer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure that the member's concerns
will be taken into consideration by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I would like to caution the member that as I understand the situation at this time there is not clear evidence of a denial of justice and that obviously in these situations one has to be veiy careful. However, the member's representations will be made known to the appropriate minister.

Madam Speaker, my question is really supplementary to the ones asked by the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys. Twice now in this House he has expressed some concern about a railway in his riding going from government ownership to private ownership.
I am wondering if the Minister of Transport would explain where the same concern had taken place in Alberta with Central Western Railway and how once it went private the service increased and improved. Would he also share the concerns about when VIA Rail left Calgary for Vancouver and what happened to that railway once it went private so that the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys does not need to believe that privatization is always bad?

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me the opportunity to express that when VIA sold part of its Rocky Mountaineer route it became a much more prosperous enterprise since it became privatized.
This is an indication that it is not to be feared if CN is offering that particular line, the Sydney-Truro, to potential bidders. It will examine the bids and will determine whether or not it is in the best interest of the region to proceed with the privatization of that line.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the acting minister of energy.
Canadian Press revealed recently that this year the federal government would subsidize the petroleum industry by about $547 million. Of course as an Albertan I
November 8, 1991

Routine Proceedings
am all for that. However that is 16 times more than the $35 million it will spend in partnerships with others to develop alternative energy sources such as wind, solar and biomass and to promote conservation.
The green plan boondoggle says that Canada is committed to stabilizing greenhouse gas emissions brought on by fossil fuel consumption by the year 2000.
Given that, how can the government or the minister of energy tilt the scales so much against renewable energy and conservation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member is well aware that the Government of Canada is committed to maintaining a level of research with respect to renewable and alternative energies in substitution for our primary energy resources.
The hon. member knows full well, particularly as an Albertan, of the importance of the fossil fuel producing industries to this country and to our national security. He understands that there are no simple alternatives and quick fixes to our dependency on fossil fuels. Notwithstanding their environmental side effects, this industry must be maintained and supported not only for the benefit of Albertans but of all Canadians.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by a number of residents of small towns, including Elginburg, Wolfe Island, Joyceville, Gananoque, Napa-nee, Harrowsmith and Sydenham, all in Ontario.

These electors are very concerned that the Government of Canada may be negotiating away article XI of the GATT They are concerned that the destruction of Canada's supply management system will destroy the dairy industry in Canada. They call upon Parliament to instruct the government to hold our Canadian system up as an example to the rest of the world and protect it entirely at all costs and to have article XI clarified and strengthened at the upcoming round of GATT negotiations.
I know that the Minister of Supply and Services, who has some farmers in his riding, will do his very best to make sure this happens and stop sitting in the House abusing people who are trying to protect the system he and his government seem to be destroying.

Madam Speaker, I have a petition signed by 7,500 Canadians from across this land asking the Canadian government to recognize the independence of Croatia and its duly elected government.
By not recognizing Croatia the Canadian government and the international community are indirectly condoning the war crimes committed by the junta in Belgrade.
I join with pride those petitioners in supporting their petition.

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to present a petition on behalf of a number of people from western Canada, Alberta and British Columbia. They are concerned about what appears to be, at least from their perspective, an increasing amount of lawlessness in the country, an increase in breaking and entering and violent crimes. They are asking the federal government to ensure that the RCMP has proper funding to enable it to carry out its mandate.

Madam Speaker, I have another petition primarily from communities throughout British Columbia. The petitioners are concerned about a plan that has been announced to divert a particular tributary of the Fraser River in an effort to move Canadian fresh water to San Diego, California.
They are simply asking that the Canadian government state that this particular proposal will not be tolerated.

Madam Speaker, it is my honour and pleasure to present a petition signed by 1,786 residents, primarily from the Toronto area, with respect to the situation in Croatia.
The gist of the petition is that Croatia instituted a democratic government in a multi-party election in April 1990.
Ninety-four per cent of the population of Croatia voted for independence. Croatians, like all other peoples, are entitled to freedom, democracy and the right to self-determination.
The petitioners therefore call on us to take the initiative in officially recognizing Croatia as an independent and sovereign democratic nation. It is a pleasure to join with them in presenting this petition.

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to present three petitions in the House today.
The first petition is signed by both women and men with respect to the goods and services tax on feminine sanitary products. They see these products as necessary. As a result they see the goods and services tax applied on these particular products as totally discriminatory.

Madam Speaker, the second petition is with respect to education and various massive cuts.
The petitioners deplore the fact that the government talks about productivity, competitiveness and a learning culture when in fact it has been incessantly cutting the educational portfolio and its financial supports.

Madam Speaker, my third petition is a petition concerning national unity.
The men and women who have signed this petition have asked the leaders of the three major political parties to ensure that this dialogue, this reaching out, ensures that Canada stays together.

Madam Speaker, I join in raising my voice with those who have read petitions with respect to the very serious situation in Croatia. There is devastation to mind, property and health of the people of that country. Men, women and children are entitled to live decently and with respect.
I table this petition asking for serious action to take place to prevent the devastation going on in Croatia. I encourage the government to participate in encouraging that action.

speechtext: With respect to the government's 1991-92 restraint measures for pay, will the restraint also apply to Crown corporations and, if not, why not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS RECEIVED BY FEDERAL POLITICAL PARTIES FOR THE YEARS 1988 TO 1990
speechtext:
The government's wage restraint measures apply directly to those Crown corporations listed in schedule II of the Public Sector Compensation Act.
All Governor in Council appointees in Crown corporations outside the purview of the Public Sector Compensation Act will also see their salaries frozen in 1991-92, and these executives will not receive performance pay in respect of their performance for this period. Following the February budget, all Crown corporations were asked to follow the spirit of the government's policy on wage restraint when concluding their collective agreements. As most of the activities of these corporations are commercial and competitive in nature, they manage their own negotiations with their own work force. Wage settlements for those corporations not directly subject to the Public Sector Compensation Act will be closely monitored.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Domm (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for Science):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I believe I had responded to the one comment made by my colleague on the other side.
The other comment from three speakers was that they really wanted to know whether this bill was slower or faster or whether I was satisfied with the government bill versus my private member's bill. The government bill is a much better bill. It includes more exclusions from the chain of appeals under extradition than even my bill did.
To be more specific, my bill versus the minister's bill put it in both tracks. It moved it over to the appeal in the Federal Court on the minister's signature or on the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and then to the superior court of the land, the Supreme Court of Canada.
In the minister's bill that moves it very rapidly from the extradition hearing to the appeal in the province. That appeal in the province then reviews the minister's signature. So the minister has a certain time frame within this legislation to sign the warrant for extradition. Then that appeal deals with it.
There is only the one appeal guaranteed on extradition under the minister's bill. There were literally two appeals, one in the Federal Court and one in the provincial court with my bill that I had introduced as Bill C-210.1 am very pleased with the minister's bill.
November 8, 1991

That answers as best I can the two questions or concerns the member had. If the member wishes to make further comment I welcome that.

Madam Speaker, I think my hon. friend should have listened more carefully to my speech and read the minister's statement. I hope he is right but I do not think he is. The minister has streamlined the procedure in the bill by intending to put the two together. Her own notes were provided by her department and on page 4 it says:
In some circumstances, however, an extradition case could appear twice before the Court of Appeal. This could happen, for example, if there was no committal order issued at the extradition hearing and this was appealed successfully by the foreign state. It could also be 1he case if there was a committal order and the Minister of Justice postponed making a decision on the surrender order until after the Court of Appeal made a decision on an appeal of that committal order, or if the Court of Appeal felt it was appropriate to deal separately with the appeal and review.
The procedure is there. The thrust of my remarks was that the minister should abandon her powers of surrender to the court so that all the determinations would be made at once by a judge instead of by a judge and then by the minister. It would avoid this multiplicity of appeals altogether. The minister's scheme should eliminate the bulk of them.
I am glad the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond is in agreement. I know the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader is in full agreement.
As I said in my speech, the minister has retained this power and there could be the two lines of appeal which follow. I think it is clear from the minister's own statements that is so.
I know the member suggested in his comments that everything was fused into one. I suggest that does not appear to be the case. I hope the committee could consider a possible change but I suspect it will be beyond their scope, given that this bill in its present form will receive second reading I presume later this day.
I appreciate the hon. member's comment and his elucidation of the principles of the bill and I am glad that the Minister of Supply and Services is so interested in the subject. I hope that he is going to make a speech instead of mumbling from his seat.
