speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (for the Minister of Justice) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-12, an act to amend the Young Offenders Act and the Criminal Code, be read the third time and passed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I know all my colleagues are pleased that we have entered the third reading debate on Bill C-12, amendments to the Young Offenders Act.
The overriding goal of the Young Offenders Act is that as many youths as possible become fully participating and contributing members of our communities as adults in accordance with the values of our society. To attain this goal, the government remains committed to the philosophy of the act that was unanimously endorsed by this House in 1982, that is that young people are responsible for their illegal behaviour and should be held accountable in a manner appropriate to their age and maturity.
Over the past few years, the federal Department of Justice has consulted on issues regarding the Young Offenders Act as seen by a wide range of persons involved with young offenders, including representatives of provincial governments and territories, corrections officials, mental health professionals, members of nongovernmental organizations concerned with juvenile justice, researchers, academics, the judiciary Crown counsel, police, defence lawyers and, of course, members of Parliament.

Government Orders
As well, the testimony of witnesses to the legislative committee that examined Bill C-12, the former Bill C-58, has proven beneficial and I think has resulted in a number of improvements to the bill. I thank my colleagues who served on that committee for their hard work.
I would like to spend a couple of minutes addressing the objectives of the Young Offenders Act in the specific context of youth charged with serious offences because it is youth charged with serious offences that I, and I am sure most members of Parliament, have had the most questions.
The provisions of the current act which have come under severest attack have been those governing the transfer to adult court of young persons charged with murder. A number of cases involving youth have attracted national attention and have influenced numerous sectors actively involved in the justice field and many members of the public believe that the transfer mechanism and sentences for murder in the Young Offenders Act should be revised. That is what we have done in this bill.
These cases called into question the integrity of the Young Offenders Act as a whole and I think have contributed to a loss of confidence in the juvenile justice system.
There are those who say that the interest of the youth should be the primary concern in accordance with the principle that young persons are not adults and therefore should not be held as accountable in the same manner or suffer the same consequences for their behaviour as adults.
There are other equally important principles in the act which refer to young persons bearing responsibility for their actions and society being afforded the necessary protection from illegal behaviour. It is the balancing of these principles which we are striving to maintain with the enactment of Bill C-12.
The objective of the federal government in these proposed amendments is to ensure that the best possible decision is made at a transfer hearing in the interest of both the youth before the court and the public.
Given the range of interpretation to date on the current test for transfer to adult court, it is viewed as highly desirable to lessen the unequal application of the test and to reinforce the notion that the rehabilitation of
the young person and the protection of the public must be weighed in determining whether or not the youth remains in the youth system.
Bill C-12 directly addresses these issues. Further, the bill specifies in the exceptional case where these objectives cannot be reconciled that the protection of the public shall be paramount.
That is what the new test says, and I think this is why Bill C-12 is such an important step forward, particularly for those who are interested in this area and for those who have lost some faith in the juvenile justice system.
Under Bill C-12, the proposed disposition for a young offender who stays in the youth system and is convicted of first or second degree murder is a maximum of five years. For those who remain in the youth system and are convicted of murder, again the maximum period is five years which is made up of three years of custody to be followed by a period of conditional supervision.
The disposition would change the maximum sentence of three years custody, a sentence which in some cases has been considered entirely inappropriate.
We have added a period of supervision in the community to help that young person get reinvolved and reintegrated into society.
The federal government has two objectives in restructuring this disposition: first, to enhance the potential for rehabilitation and, second, to offer increased security to the community at large.
In proposing a period of guidance and supervision in the community after a period of custody, the bill recognizes that the protection of the public and rehabilitation go hand in hand.
However, the custodial term could be extended where a court is satisfied that the young person is likely to commit an offence causing serious harm or death. Additionally a youth court may order the return of a young person to custody where there has been a violation of a condition of release.
Bill C-12 also reduces the period of parole in eligibility for young offenders who are transferred to adult court and convicted of murder. Transferred youths convicted of first or second degree murder would receive a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, but the period at which time they would become eligible for parole would be between five and ten years.
November 8, 1991

Such a reduced period of parole ineligibility to be determined by the judge at the time of sentencing would diminish the negative effects of long-term incarceration and would reflect the belief that a young person has the potential for rehabilitation.
At report stage, the government tabled a motion concerning the placement of youth whose cases have been transferred to adult court. That particular motion was passed by the House.
This motion responds to the concerns of many members of Parliament and of individuals and organizations with the current placement of youth in adult facilities.
While the government had initially intended to deal with this issue as part of a second phase of legislative review, time has afforded the opportunity to consult further and resolve the issue at this stage.
The provision that I just referred to would require as the normal rule the placement of a transferred youth under the age of 18 in youth facilities during the pre-trial stage.
An exception could be made and the youth could be placed in an adult facility where a youth court is satisfied, taking into account the best interests of the youth and the safety of other youth, that this is desirable.
A youth over the age of 18 years would normally be placed in an adult facility. A provision is also made for an exception allowing the court to order placement in a youth facility using the same criteria.
Where a youth is transferred and convicted in adult court and is under 18 years, provision is made for the court to select between youth, provincial adult and adult penitentiary systems having to take into account a number of factors. Beyond this bill further changes to the Young Offenders Act are being examined to address three distinct aspects of the act. These are, first, to respond more effectively to the special needs of adolescents given their state of dependency and level of development and maturity; second, to determine the most appropriate legislative framework for custodial sentences and for sentence review; and, third, to ascertain the most suitable provisions regarding the admissibility into evidence of statements made by young people to persons in authority.
At the heart of the sentencing amendments is the question of how sentences should be structured to achieve the greatest promise of rehabilitation. The
Government Orders
government is committed to moving ahead as quickly as possible with whatever legislative changes are desirable to realize this goal.
In conclusion, the greatest challenge to Canada's juvenile justice system arises where young people are involved in the commission of serious or violent offences, particularly murder. Parliament's role in meeting this challenge is to enact sound juvenile justice legislation which adheres to the principles and policies embodied in the Young Offenders Act. Bill C-12 exemplifies such legislation. The bill reinforces the premise that the protection of the public and rehabilitation can go hand in hand. Both of these objectives would be enhanced, in our opinion, by a follow-up period of community supervision.
In exceptional cases where the juvenile justice system cannot protect the public or rehabilitate the young offender within the time available in the youth system, as I have indicated, the protection of the public becomes paramount under this new bill. The transfer test makes this very clear.
I think that is something that for the most part most Canadians are enthusiastic about and one of the reasons I believe for those who are aware and concerned about the whole juvenile justice system to applaud the provisions of Bill C-12.
The bill also recognizes the potential for rehabilitation for those youth transferred to the adult system by allowing for their earlier integration into the community. I think it is a step forward in this whole question of the transfer of young people from youth court to the adult system.
Again I congratulate and thank all my colleagues who have worked so hard on Bill C-12 as well as other pieces of legislation in the justice area. I think all of this contributes to the confidence of people in the system. All of them contribute ultimately to making Canada a safer and a better place in which to live.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the thanks of the parliamentary secretary. I respect the parliamentary secretary. I know he did not want to waste his thanks on me. I have been a member of Parliament for 12 years and I can say without hesitation that this is the worst bill that has ever come from the Department of Justice. It is absolute trash and it is not going to do the job that needs to be done.

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
The member says he applauds those who have supported this bill. One witness who came before the legislative committee supported this bill. Every other witness, and there were many, said this was bad legislation.
Even the minister does not support this bill if you look at the facts. Where is she? The minister did not come to the legislative committee once. The parliamentary secretary says it is his job. I would like to ask where responsible government is if the minister is not going to support her own legislation. Where is responsible government if we cannot actually get to the minister to put our concerns through? When I spoke to the minister about this she said: "My parliamentary secretary is advising me as to what has happened. I have officials from the department who are there". That is not acceptable. That is not the same thing as the minister being there to hear concerns first hand.
Also the minister assured us that she would be here for third reading. All she had to do is read a speech. She is not here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has been in this House for a long time, as he has said himself. He does know that referring to the presence or absence of a member or a minister should not be done. I would appreciate if he would take another line of questioning in his speech. The hon. member.

Madam Speaker, I certainly do not mind taking another line. I have quite a few of them here.
The bill itself is very misleading. When you look at Bill C-12 it says: "First reading on May 29, 1991". That would give you the impression that this bill was presented to the House as recently as May of 1991 and has proceeded quickly.
I want to tell the House that nothing could be further from the truth. The reason that we have a first reading date on the bill of May 29, 1991 is because we started a new session. The first reading of the bill was over a year ago. In fact, we completed the legislative committee proceedings on this bill in December 1990. We are now in third reading over nine months after we completed the legislative committee process. There has been absolutely no rush.
In a letter dated September 25 which was sent to many people the minister says that she is now proceeding to improve other aspects of the bill. She hopes to bring forward legislation and the parliamentary secretary referred to the same thing, "other aspects of the bill". She says:
-given the public and government consultation that has already occurred on many of these issues, it is hoped that the next phase can be conducted in as short a time period as possible; accordingly, responses from the non-governmental sector are being requested no later than December 1, 1991.
The natural thing is to suggest to the minister that if she feels this is an imperfect bill why is she presenting it to the House at the present time? Second, if she felt that there were other things necessary for the improvement of this bill, why were they not put into this bill after the legislative committee process? We just had report stage a few weeks ago. There is no reason why the government could not have brought forward amendments at the report stage to improve this bill so we would have a better bill.
The parliamentary secretary says that the government brought forward an amendment which would ease the concerns of a great many people. I can assure you that it does not. The fact is that in one way it is somewhat of an improvement. What the amendment does is say that those youth who are waiting for the question of whether they will be transferred to an adult court or heard in a youth court will be kept separate and apart from adult prisoners in a special youth facility. It is great that they can stay in this facility until the age of 20. That is wonderful. That helps.
But what does it do for the young people who are convicted of the offence subsequent to having their case heard for which they have been charged? In this motion it says that the youth will be kept in a youth facility, kept in a minimum security facility or sentenced to a penitentiary. It does absolutely nothing to look after the question of how the youth are to be treated after they are convicted.
The only reason we have this amendment is because the government has been embarrassed that the bill did not meet the terms of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child which this government co-sponsored with another nation. In fact the Prime Minister was in New
November 8, 1991

York representing one of the two co-sponsoring nations which signed this declaration.
Section 37(3) says that young people have to be kept separate and apart from adults unless it is in their best interests to be so. It directly refers to the incarceration of young offenders and says that they are not to be kept with adult prisoners.
The government could not ratify this document with that in there so it brought forward this motion. But it still does not erase the inconsistency that exists between this legislation and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child because young offenders are still going to be incarcerated with adult prisoners after they are finally charged.
Young offenders in youth court will now be given longer sentences and will have the date for parole reduced to 10 years if they are convicted of first degree murder and have a 25-year sentence. This makes it more palatable for courts to refer young offenders to an adult court. It is an invitation to refer these offenders to an adult court. This is counterproductive to what is really needed in society today if we are going to deal with the problem and youth.
Let me just run over the procedure as it exists. First we have a situation where a young offender commits a crime. The young offender is held in a holding institution. Quite often the Crown prosecutor will make a motion to have that young offender referred to an adult institution and that the case will not be heard in youth court.
If the Crown prosecutor is successful the young offender can then appeal. Then there could be another appeal whereupon the question of whether the young offender is guilty or not guilty of the crime will not be heard for as long as two years. The young person is in incarceration for two years before his or her case actually comes before the courts to determine his or her guilt or innocence.
In this case the amendment looks after the fact that the young person must be held separate and apart. The problem is that is only a part of the problem. What happens to the young offender later? Where does the young offender go after his or her case is finally heard?
Government Orders
The other incidence is this. What happens while the young person is in a holding institution? There was a recent case decided where six young people were charged with the gang rape of a 14-year old girl. The question of whether these six young people were going to be tried in a youth court or an adult court took two years to resolve.
Finally it was decided that the young people would be tried in a youth court. The problem was that it took two years. We look at this unnecessary procedure and we look at the recent Askov decision. There was an appeal under the charter after this two year matter was finally resolved which found that this process took too long and it violated the rights of the six young men to a fair trial. The court found in favour of this under the Askov decision. These six young people were let go. They were not even tried for the gang rape with which they had been charged. They are out on the street. Can you image the parents of this then 14-year old girl and their vision of what the justice system is doing to right the wrong that had occurred? They would be absolutely apoplectic at that decision.
With these transfer provisions under the Askov case, lawyers will be appealing the decisions for transfer to an adult court. That could go on for as much as two years. It does not even have to go on for two years. It can go on for a much shorter period of time. The judges will rule that the young person's right to a fair trial has been violated and these young people are going to go free. That is a travesty. It is an absolute travesty. To those out there who say: "No, it is never going to happen" I say just look at the court records. Fifty thousand cases in Canada have been thrown out under the Askov case because the period of time it took this person to come to trial was considered by the judge to be too long.
The projection is that at least 100,000 cases are going to be thrown out. A person called me and was in tears because there was a case of a drunken driver hitting and killing a young person. It is absolutely ridiculous that the government is promoting these transfer provisions.
Let me talk about the violation of the rights of the defendant, if we want to look at it that way. As it stands right now, in an appeal for a transfer provision the young

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
person has to plead guilty or not guilty. If the young person pleads not guilty the court psychologists who have been appointed will say: "Oh, well, if the young person is pleading not guilty, he or she is not repentant, so there is no hope of rehabilitation for this young person". We are going to send them to an adult institution where there will be less chance of rehabilitation. That weighs on the report to the judge and the judge's decision.
What young persons should be penalized for saying they are not guilty if they really believe they are not guilty? It is a violation of their fundamental rights.
Second, if young persons say they are guilty what does that do for the final disposition of their case when the final matter for which they are charged is heard? Certainly it is going to have an effect. It is absolutely ludicrous to have these transfer provisions. The government is only increasing the likelihood that there are going to be more.
The transfer provisions are really ludicrous because they are applied in different ways in different parts of the country. In Quebec, only 15 per cent of young offenders is transferred to an adult institution.
In one of the western provinces the figure is 87 per cent. Why? It is because there are more native young offenders in that provinces.
It is a travesty that this is going on in this country at the present time.
What about rehabilitation? We are told by the parliamentary secretary and the minister: "This is all going to come to pass. This is going to occur". I am not convinced. Rehabilitation and guidance for young people is a provincial jurisdiction. When the Young Offenders Act was passed in 1984 it was with the belief that the provinces would provide institutions for young offenders separate and apart from adults and they would provide rehabilitation and counselling for these young offenders. It has not happened. In fact, the inclination has been to put more and more of them in adult institutions.
The parliamentary secretary says that the first priority of this bill is public safety and that people applaud that. Of course they applaud that. People are scared to death to walk the streets in many parts of our cities right now.
They want more public safety but they also want a workable process. If you take a young offender, put him in an adult institution where he is abused by adult criminals and sexually abused constantly day after day, that person is going to be a person who has a grudge against society. He may want to get back at society.
Second, you are going to have a former prisoner who has learned pretty well every trick in the book on how to commit his or her next crime.
There absolutely has to be rehabilitation. I want to refer to a man I have a great deal of respect for, Maurice Rose. He is originally from my constituency in Cape Breton Island. He wrote a notice and distributed it to all members of Parliament.
He says: "Let me begin by introducing myself. I am Maurice Rose of LaSalle, Quebec. On March 17, 1989 my wife and I left for North Sydney, Cape Breton for what was to be a very short trip. On the morning of March 19, 1989 I received a call informing me that my son, Joe, had been murdered on the MUCTC bus at 3.30 a.m. that same day by four armed youths with knives".
He would be a man you would expect to want to get back at every youth offender in Canada. However he has distributed a petition across this country asking for further punishment, certainly more realistic punishment, but also treatment and rehabilitation for young offenders. He is a man who in his grief has said that the system is not working. He has also said that what this government is proposing is not working.
He has distributed a petition across this country which has 800,000 signatures. It has 800,000 signatures. The man, in his grief over losing his son two years ago, has done more to bring to the attention of this country the problem that exists in our cities and with our young people than everyone in the Department of Justice. Certainly that includes the minister.
We have to depend on our citizens who have received this kind of hurt. What is going to happen to this country? The Department of Justice used to be one of the gleaming examples of effectiveness in government. Today it is diminished considerably because it is not leading the fight on crime in Canada. No, not at all. It is following.
November 8, 1991

As it takes two steps forward and one step back and in this case one step forward and two steps back, crime is becoming more sophisticated. It is more sophisticated. The danger to our citizens and to our municipalities is increasing.
Let me just quote one article from The Ottawa Sun. This does not rely on whether you like The Ottawa Sun or not. It is pure statistics. It says: "The number of teenage girls charged with violent crimes in Ontario has doubled since the Young Offenders Act was introduced, police figures show. There were 65 per cent more teenage boys charged with violent crimes in 1990 than in 1986". That is a 65 per cent increase in four years.
Federally there was a 34 per cent increase in violent crime among youth in the other nine provinces and two territories. Across Canada there was a 34 per cent increase in four years. We have a very, very serious situation here. I just want to mention one thing.
We say that the young people need to be considered in this very important area.
Madam Speaker, let me tell you what the Minister of Justice said. She said too many young people "turn to crime because they are not finding their way in the education system and not finding their way in productive ways in society".
Madam Minister, it is a good guess but you have missed the mark by a mile. How can you expect the minister to introduce meaningful legislation if she does not even know the problem?
I want to quote from one very eminent psychiatrist in Ontario's Thistletown Regional Centre, Dr. Clive Chamberlain. He says: "The Young Offenders Act not only fails to ensure that kids who commit murder will get the psychiatric help they need. It does not protect the public from potentially dangerous criminals. Predicting whether a child is capable of an act of murder is like predicting an earthquake". That is very accurate.
The minister says: "No, that is not the case. They turn to crime because they are not finding their way in the education system and not finding their way in productive ways in society".
Government Orders
There are a great many young people from good homes and high income families committing crimes. An alarming number of them are highly educated. There are certainly a lot of young people who turn to crime from single parent families and are out all day with no supervision. A lot of them do not have a chance. They are ideal for those who want to exert bad influences on them.
To say that it is because they are not finding their way in the education system-talk to the teachers in the large cities in this country teaching students up to 17 years of age. They are scared to death. Young people are going to school, nine and ten-year-olds, carrying firearms. In one case the school expelled the students. They were ten and eleven-year-olds carrying firearms and bringing them to school.
Do you know what happened, Madam Speaker? The school did not get credit for that. It got calls from the neighbourhood saying: "Why are you putting these children out on the streets where they are a danger to the neighbourhood?" What are the teachers supposed to do? Allow students who are carrying handguns in school, at the age of 10 and 11? It is absolutely ludicrous.
What does this government do? Does it address the minimum age, which is 12 under the Young Offenders Act, and the fact that anyone under 12 is not considered culpable for a crime? No. You have to be 12 years old before you are even considered eligible to be under the jurisdiction of the Young Offenders Act.
There are sophisticated criminals on the streets who are 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 years of age. Let us look at this. All we are doing with this legislation is leading people into a false sense of security. It is absolutely irresponsible but this is what is being done.
Where is organized crime in this question? Madam Speaker, let me tell you where organized crime is. Organized crime is promoting young offenders. It sees that young offenders are committing crimes, going to court, getting a slap on the wrist and a little stem talking to by the judge and then they are out on the streets. Sometimes when they are convicted they are back on the streets in a few months.

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
How can you expect young people to have respect for our criminal justice system? They are laughing at us. They are laughing at the police, and with good reason. They are getting away with it. Organized crime is putting these young people up front. They are the foot soldiers in organized crime because it knows if the young people are caught they will get away with a minor sentence. Let me say something else. Do not let me leave the impression that I am insensitive to young criminals, because nothing could be further from the truth. We have a real problem here. I want to say that doing what this bill recommends, doing what this government wants us to do without meaningful amendments to the Young Offenders Act, is only going to exacerbate the problem.
We have to take these young people and give them some rehabilitation. Some of them just do not understand. I talked to psychiatrists that say that young people commit murders and they do not even know what they have done, they are so mixed up. That is hard to believe. It is hard for me to believe, but this is what I am told. There are an awful lot of mixed up young people out there and a lot of them have never had a chance.
One can say: "Oh, well, he killed somebody and what chance did that person have", but let me say that attitude is not going to correct the problem. We need longer sentences. We have to have longer sentences. We cannot let these young people out after a few months because they need counselling, they need rehabilitation. If we have young persons in a facility for just a year or a few months, how are we going to give them meaningful rehabilitation? We cannot take a young person aside and say: "You must have counselling and rehabilitation", because the young person could say: "To heck with you. Go find somebody else to give your sermon to. I am not getting any counselling". So the young person is out on the street.
What is needed is for the young person to realize that he or she needs this counselling. That may take time, but we cannot allow these young people out on the street until they realize that they are in need of help and that they can get this help. This is for their safety, because they are young persons and they are going to be back.
Even if they commit first degree or second degree murder and even if they get sentenced to 25 years, they are going to be back on the street and they are going to be out in society. We do not want them to be bitter. We do not want them to say: "I am getting even with society because of the way I have been treated". We want them to be meaningful, important members of society. We just cannot afford to have these young people coming out and committing more crimes again. It is mushrooming. We have to do something realistic.
What we in the Liberal Party are saying is: Do not go with these transfers. Do not transfer young people to adult court. Have a unified family and youth court which knows of the young persons and their parents or parent or guardian from the time they were young. There is a history in the family court perhaps of family problems and problems with the youth and these judges can deal with it. They are trained in family problems and youth problems. Of course now a family court cannot deal with a jury trial, but that can be changed. There is no reason that a jury trial cannot be the privilege of the young person if he or she wants it.
There are also going to be incorrigibles. The person who said there is no such thing as a bad child was off the mark. There are young people-maybe it is not their own fault-who now are beyond counselling. That is a tough decision to make I know. I even find it difficult to say that some young person is beyond counselling. However there are cases where we have to make that decision. There are young persons who cannot be put in a youth facility because to do so is not going to help the people there who we feel can be helped. Perhaps we have to put such young persons in an adult institution. I am sorry, but perhaps that has happen in those few special cases.
The fact is that a youth court can still do that. There is no reason that we cannot give the youth family court the power to sentence someone to an adult institution if it feels he or she is incorrigible. The youth judge is a lot more able to do that than the regular judge who has not had this special history in dealing with family and youth problems. There is no reason we cannot have that court doing that.

We also feel that sentences in the youth court should be increased, for instance, for first and second degree murder. It is up to 10 years for first degree murder and 7 years for second degree murder. Sure, give longer sentences. Any psychiatrist or any counsellor who deals with young people says: "I do not like longer sentences. I do not think they help". Believe me, longer sentences are preferable to putting these people in adult institutions because if we do that, we have lost them. They say: "We admit there are cases where you have to have a longer period of time to reach these young people and then to give them the proper counselling". I feel that longer sentences are important. What we are trying to do is deal with something that will have a meaningful result.
I find it galling that this government has been in power for seven years. In 1984 the Prime Minister answered a questionnaire from the Canadian Council on Children and Youth. He was asked about the priorities of the Conservative government in the area of young offenders and he said: "The Progressive Conservative Party supported passage of the Young Offenders Act and continues to endorse its philosophy and principles. We are committed to assuring financial assistance to the provinces to allow for equal application of the law and availability of programs and services across Canada".
Those are empty words.

Those are empty words. Nothing could be further from the truth. In fact in 1989 the government froze assistance to the provinces in this regard for a five-year period.
We have a deteriorating situation in this country. People in our municipalities are scared to walk the streets, are fearful of the increased rate of crime and are buying firearms, which we definitely do not want them to do but which they are doing in response to the increasing crime rate.
We have police that have to deal with this without the satisfactory laws to allow them to do the job. We have counsellors and psychologists that want to help these young people but cannot do it because the governments will not give them any money.
It is nice that governments can build hospitals and schools and say at election time: "We have these lovely hospitals and schools". Of course the hospitals may not be staffed properly. They may not have the proper equipment. One or two floors may be closed because they do not want to spend the money to outfit and staff them properly. They point to hospitals because people
Government Orders
like hospitals. They feel a security from having proper hospitalization and proper education.
However, they will not spend it for young offenders' facilities. Why? It is because it shows that there is a little frailty in all of us and that if they build young offenders' facilities they are admitting to the public that there is a human failing, that perhaps some young people are going to need guidance, assistance and incarceration for a period of time. That is a bad message; that is a downer at election time.
We in this country are suffering from the shortsightedness of governments and their underestimation of the Canadian public. I also want to say that if we do not do something to address this matter, we are not only going to have a serious problem on our hands; we are going to have a catastrophic problem on our hands.
We have seen just south of the border what happens. We have to do something constructive to deal with the problems of increasing crime but, more important, the increasing crime among our young people. We have to do something constructive. This bill is not constructive. It is a retrogressive step. The fact that this should come forward at a time when we need the government on our side, to me is absolutely galling.
I just cannot say strongly enough how disappointed I am and how disappointed Canadians are going to be when they see and realize the hollowness of this legislation.
I want to say to the government in one final plea: please, please withdraw this legislation and bring forward something that is constructive and that is going to be meaningful in the fight against crime, aiding the people of this country, protecting and perhaps helping the young people who need this help, and at the same time giving the greater protection the government says it wants to give to the public. Please withdraw this legislation and bring forward something constructive.
This is just a terrible piece of legislation. I want to say as strongly as I possibly can that our party will not support this legislation. It is a disgrace. We demand that the government reconsider it and bring forward something that is going to be meaningful.

Mr. Speaker, I rise as my party's justice critic, as the NDP justice critic, to speak on this very important bill respecting amendments to the Young Offenders Act.
I think this is about the 19th time I have been up this week. I am sure other members and people who are watching are probably thinking: "Well, there is that fellow again. I thought they were going to get rid of him about a week ago". Of course I would not have wished

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
this, but I am beginning to think if they had suspended me from the House for a couple of weeks it certainly would have improved my health. Who knows, after the members had heard all my 19 speeches, it might have improved their health too.
In any case I think this is the last one. As the Chair knows, we are going to be spending the next week with our constituents and so we will get some feedback hopefully on some of these justice bills.
I want to say right away that I want to make three points. The first point is that this is a very limited bill. Indeed it is a wrong-headed bill to deal with a very big problem, and that is the growing difficulties with juvenile crime and the rehabilitation of juveniles in this country.
The second point I want to make is that I want to be positive. I do not just want to be negative. There is another approach to deal with this and I want to offer some of my views and the views of my party about what the other approach would be.
Third, I want to be straightforward and say this is the last part of a phoney war that we have seen this week, a phoney public relations war. It has not been a real campaign against crime but a PR campaign against crime: issue a press release or have a press conference as this government has been doing all week in the so-called protection of society agenda, or law and order week as it has been dubbed. It thinks that resurrecting some old bills and doing some press releases somehow is going to fight increased crime in Canada. I say to the government and to the minister it is just not going to work. The Canadian people are not stupid. They can see through that.
Indeed I will give a little example here. The minister had a press conference with other ministers to which he invited us and the media to come to talk about this agenda. At the same time on the Hill today and yesterday there is a man, a Mr. Maurice Rose to whom the hon. member from Cape Breton made reference, whose son was killed in a tragic event. A number of juveniles were involved and Mr. Rose feels quite strongly, I think with good reason, that justice was not done in the sentencing of those people. Mr. Rose asked to meet the minister. He met with the hon. member, the justice critic of the Liberal Party. He met with me this morning. He
asked to meet the minister but the minister did not have time to meet him. They passed in the hall.
This is the mistake of the minister and the mistake of this government. It is all glitz, it is all PR, but it is not people.
All tactics and no substance.

"All tactics and no substance", as the member from Broadview-Greenwood just said. He put his finger right on it.
That is the problem with this government. Wake up, there are people out there in this country. They have real needs. You cannot fight crime by press releases. It does not work. It is phoney and it is dishonest.
I said another approach could be used in juvenile cases and I think it is incumbent upon us to put forward that approach. I will come to it when I am a little further into my speech. We could treat juveniles as juveniles.
We should not be afraid to punish them. We could be tough. There could be short, sharp punishment for offences. We should not be afraid of incarceration. We should beef up treatment facilities and so on.
Once you put a juvenile in adult jail, God, that is a school for crime. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca who worked as a social worker until he was fired by the old Bennett government in British Columbia decided not to get mad, but to get even, so he became premier of the province and got rid of the government that fired him. He made a good point in an earlier debate here.
He said: "You put a young man who is 15, 16 or 17 in an adult jail and they are going to be raped within days. They are going to be criminals within six months to a year. They are going to learn all the tactics". We have to deal with juveniles as juveniles, I believe, but we must have the facilities to do it and we have to not be afraid of not having tough punishment also for juveniles as juveniles.
If the Prime Minister would read his own speeches at the United Nations, he would notice that he says one thing at the UN in the great light of world opinion and then brings in a different bill here, although he has amended this bill somewhat to conform with the speech at the UN but not completely.


November 8, 1991

Anyway, there is another way of dealing with juvenile crime. The other thing is not only should the minister talk to the families of victims like Mr. Rose. She should talk to some of the people who came before our committee who wanted a vastly changed bill. Instead, we got a very limited bill.
What this bill has, just to summarize it for the House, is three objectives: to make it easier to transfer a youth to adult court, to increase the penalty for youth convicted in youth court of first or second degree murder from three years to five years less a day, and to permit earlier parole eligibility for youths transferred to adult court on murder charges.
It is a very narrow bill dealing with very few of the real problems that we have, as the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys pointed out in his excellent speech.
Rather than reiterate some of the things he said, I want to emphasize a couple of the amendments that I proposed that were ruled out of order. I offer them in third reading as a potential for talking about later on or bringing a new bill and really dealing with the subject, not the PR war but the real war as I call it.
The first one is reference to an amendment I proposed about a statement of principles in the bill. I wanted to amend the statement of principles as set out in section 3 of the Young Offenders Act to affirm the principle of giving cultural needs, especially of native youth, special consideration in the delivery of services, programs and facilities for young offenders and to affirm for the first time in the Young Offenders Act that the principle of rehabilitation of young offenders best serves the interests of society.
I was particularly concerned by some evidence that we received in committee from the Canadian Council of Children and Youth. I will quote from pages 24 and 25 of its brief to the committee on what was then Bill C-58: "Consideration should be given to improving the act's declaration of principle found in section 3. These principles are sometimes cited by court, policy makers and politicians and probably influence the outcome of individual cases, and policy decisions.
Government Orders
They also have important symbolic value for youth, professionals, politicians and society as a whole. The long-term protection of financial interests in society are best served by the rehabilitation of young offenders and their successful reintegration into society".
"And their successful reintegration into society" is the end that we are all trying for.
The council pointed out that the declaration of principle explicitly acknowledged that the interests of society are best served by the rehabilitation of young offenders and their successful reintegration into society.
That was in the statement. That could conceivably require the provinces and the federal government to provide real facilities for young offenders, and it would be there in the law. They would be required to do that.
The council also has a concern that services, programs and facilities for young offenders must be culturally appropriate. In particular, in many places services for aboriginal youth are not appropriate to their values, culture or language. In a number of provinces child welfare legislation contains a declaration of principle to the effect that services and programs for youth must be provided in a culturally appropriate fashion and in particular one that recognizes the special needs of aboriginal youth.
There are too many youths in our adult jails and this is a tragedy in Canada. We never really recognized that and dealt with it in the bill. That is a smaller area but a really important area.
There is another area that we were unable to get into the bill. Because of the way the system works, you get a narrow bill and you hear witnesses. You realize what needs to be done in the juvenile system, as the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys pointed out, and then you try to bring in the amendments but they never get in because you only can amend the particular bill. That is why we need new legislation. We should strike now while we are very well aware, unless of course you want to fight a PR war on crime. If you want to fight a real war then you start getting some real amendments.
Here is another one. This again comes from the recommendation of the Canadian Council on Children and Youth. It said in its brief to the committee on Bill

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
C-58: "There should be an ongoing national research and discussion in the area of juvenile justice. The council favours the establishment of a national institute for juvenile justice to undertake ongoing research, stimulate informed public and professional dialogue and take the lead in professional education and training. Such an institute would require federal funding to be a viable venture. A number of other countries have such a national juvenile justice institute".
It went on to say: "We have incomplete information at this time on the impact of the Young Offenders Act on the numbers of youth in custody, the numbers of youth diverted in the alternate measures program and so on. Because of the incompleteness of the information this bill is premature and ill-considered. We should get the information before we proceed. To do so, we must make it compulsory that all jurisdictions in Canada collect and report to the institute statistical information respecting arrests, charges, diversions, alternate measures and custodial disposition".
Of course, that would mean not fighting a PR campaign, would it not? That would mean getting some real information. That would mean really starting to build a workable bill. There is another amendment that could be considered.
I said the government was not listening. I mentioned Mr. Rose. I just want to read the letter that Mr. Maurice Rose is writing to members of Parliament. Let me read it and put it on the record: "Let me begin by introducing myself. I am Maurice Rose of LaSalle, Quebec. On March 17, 1989 my wife and I left for North Sydney, Cape Breton for what was to be a very short trip. On the morning of March 19,1989 I received a call informing me that my son Joe had been murdered at an MUCTC bus stop at 3.30 a.m. of that day by four youths armed with knives".
I think it was at the Frontenac metro station, on March 19, 1989, in Montreal: "Of the youth that killed my son the 19-year-old was tried in adult court and was sentenced to seven years. One 15-year-old received a sentence of three years in a youth home. The other 15-year-old was sentenced to 11 months and the 14-year-old to six months. It must be noted that in the case of the 14-year-old the social worker held a foot-high file and clearly informed the judge that this young offender was a danger to society. It took the judge a
mere 15 minutes to render a judgment which amounts to a mere slap on the wrist, a joke.
I wish to inform you of my fervent opposition to Bill C-12. Included herewith you will find a copy of a petition I have circulated across Canada. To date over 800,000 signatures appear on this petition to present it to the Minister of Justice, Kim Campbell", who would not even meet with this man, "thereby providing that the people of Canada also wish stricter measures taken toward young offenders.
I have also appeared before the committee. I am doing this without any financial backing. Hence I implore you to vote against Bill C-12.
The Young Offenders Act is far too lenient on youngsters having committed a crime. These individual need special assistance and guidance to ensure that the cycle is broken, so that they too can lead a responsible life in our society.
I realize that changes to the Young Offenders Act will not bring back my son. I do hope however that justice will be served for other youngsters and their families across the country who may also experience the pain and anguish my family and I have felt".
Mr. Maurice Rose can be reached at Box 664, Champlain Station, LaSalle, Quebec. I put that forward to the House and to the Canadian public so that they can help Mr. Rose in his battle. Mr. Rose spoke to the press. There is a good article in The Montreal Gazette of Wednesday, March 20, 1991, by Jack Todd where he says: "You know, first I ran into brick walls but the biggest brick wall was Ottawa and Kim Campbell refused to see him". He said: "Some people get it wrong. They think I am out to hurt kids. I am not out to hurt kids. I want them to get help. I want it mandatory and I want some facilities to help them". Here is a man pouring his heart out to Parliament and telling us to do something more than just PR, to do some real things about young offenders.
I said that this bill does three things. It makes it easier to transfer to adult court. The problem of course is that if you put a young offender in adult court and the adult system, the treatment facilities are not available and so this transfer means an abandonment of the youth.
The bill deals with a very small amount of people. We are dealing with murder charges which represents one-

fortieth of one per cent of all offences dealt with in youth court. That is a pretty small amount to deal with.
I had a meeting in my riding in a high school in which they discussed youth gangs. There was so much more to discuss rather than transfer on murder applications, but we do not have that in the bill.
The bill also deals with detention provisions and we mentioned this. I recognize that the government accepted an amendment that I first presented in committee in which we tried to keep young offenders separated from adults. I have some concerns whether that is going to work out in practice and I think we are going to have to look at this amendment. We passed it very quickly. It changes very much at the last moment and I think we are going to have to watch that and see how it is working. I flag that for the government.
There is also a provision in the bill for parole eligibility. You can get earlier parole if desired, but we should not confuse that because earlier parole has nothing to do with what it is like to be in an adult jail, which I said is a school for criminals.
I could go on and talk about this bill for a long time. We had a lot of evidence on the bill.
Perhaps I should bring my remarks to a conclusion and say that this is a very, very limited bill on a very important topic. There was another way to proceed. We could have really dealt with juveniles, kept them in the juvenile system, beefed up the juvenile system, short, sharper penalties, longer penalties in the juvenile system, decent facilities, psychiatric treatment when it was mentioned; that is what we could have done. Instead, we get a Willie Norton approach, if I can call it that. It is all PR and they are trying to convince the Canadian public this week that this government has met a kind of law and order agenda. Well it is all PR. It is just not so. If you look at this thin bill you will see that it is not really dealt with.
The minister says she will consult now. She had better have a new round of consultation with the people who work in this system. I think there is evidence in this bill that there has been no consultation.
If you really want to have a crime agenda and not a PR agenda, if you want to really attack crime you attack illiteracy. If you really want to attack crime, you attack child abuse. If you really want to attack crime, you attack poverty. If you really want to attack crime, you attack
Government Orders
unemployment. If you really want to attack crime, you get to the root of it by having a decent juvenile system that works.
The problems of youth crime are not easy ones to address, but we must resist the temptation to supply simple solutions for complex problems. Increasing sentences, building more jails and eliminating the distinction between children and adults may appeal to public fears, but that approach does nothing for real treatment, nothing for the protection of the community and nothing for services to the victim. All you do is guarantee a steady, unending supply of adult criminals in the future. That is what this bill does and that is why we oppose this bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to direct the hon. member's mind to two points that he made. He mentioned the lack of consultation on this bill. I would suggest to the hon. member that there was considerable consultation that I mentioned in my remarks to the House. I think the proof of that consultation was the support that we found at the committee stage of this bill.
I would remind all hon. members that this bill was in large part supported by the Canadian Bar Association and by the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police.
I am not saying that everybody totally supported it. That is part of the committee process. But the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police support the thrust of what we are doing here along with the two representatives the committee heard from the judiciary. They had suggestions and in fairness it should be said that most were related to the second phase that the government has proposed on this. Most of the suggestions or criticisms that were given were directed toward the second part of this.
But the two members of the judiciary and the Canadian Council of Youth found positive aspects in this.

Mr. Speaker, I take great exception to talking about the second phase of a bill we have never seen and something of which we have never heard.
How many times have we heard that somebody is going to do something and bring forward other legislation? There is no second phase before this House and I resent any mention of it as if he knew what he was talking about.

November 8, 1991
Government Orders

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think what the hon. member resents most is that I am calling him to task on his comments that this bill was not supported at the committee stage. He said nobody supported it with the exception of one witness. He said the minister did not support this. The hon. member knows this is not factual. The Minister of Justice is obviously very supportive. This is her bill and her government's bill. This is our bill. She is very supportive of it.
I bring it back to the hon. member for Port Moody- Coquitlam. I suggest to him that we found substantial support at the committee stage and I think that was as a result of the consultation process.
I want him to direct his attention to one other matter. Most of this bill deals with the transfer provisions and the penalties for young people who are convicted of murder. Toward the end of his speech the hon. member said: "What young people need are short sharp sentences". I would like him to clarify this. Was he referring, as this bill does, in large part to those convicted of murder? Was he referring to short sharp sentences for them?
Would he not agree that if we followed the suggestion of the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys for these longer sentences and keeping them in the youth system we would have a situation where we would have 24 and 25-year-olds who get this long sentence. In effect we would have adults with young people, 14 and 15-year-olds. That may not be exactly what the United Nations had in mind when it said separating young people is not always in the best interest of young people who might remain in the youth system detention facilities for a period of 10 years.
I would ask him to address the two parts.

With reference to the latter part on short sharp sentences I meant for other juvenile crimes which we could not deal with because the bill does not deal with it. The bill deals with about one-fortieth of one per cent of all the offences. The government did not really deal with that. I think there should be adequate sentences for murder of course.
I did not say the government did not consult with people on the bill. I said that there would be further consultations and that government should listen.
There is one person the government did not consult with. The hon. Minister of Justice was asked to meet with a truck driver from Cape Breton who came to the Hill. She would not meet with him. She would rather have a press conference on the PR aspects of the week. This is what it is all about. This man came and he does not have a limo. He is a truck driver. He does not have an executive assistant. Sorry. He is just a ordinary truck driver from Cape Breton. He has no millions of bucks like this government spends on PR. He is just a truck driver who lost his kid, that is all. He has none of these big PR assistants or executive assistants to do things. He is just a little guy in grief and she would not even meet with him. That is how much they think of the Canadian people. That is their problem. They do not care about people and that is why they are going to get thrown out at the earliest opportunity Canadians get.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to ask my hon. friend from Port Moody-Coquitlam a question. He has done a good deal of work on this case and worked hard on the committee. It is my understanding that while there might have been some parts of this legislation that some of the witnesses did approve, there was only one witness who approved this bill and felt this was sufficient to go forward as it was, without major changes.
I do not ask the hon. member to remember but the consensus from committee was this bill needed more work and that it was not satisfactory. I would like to know his feelings on it.

I could not agree more. What has happened in some of these justice bills as they come forward is that when we started hearing about the bills they were quite narrow. This bill deals with three aspects of the Young Offenders Act. We kept hearing about a lot of other things that need to be done.
In the Young Offenders Act I mentioned the justice institute, native kids, better facilities and co-operation with the provinces.
In the gun control bill which was one of the good things we passed this week we had evidence that there is now a problem with legally buying restricted handguns in cities. That was just coming out in this evidence.
November 8, 1991

We need another justice round. I think we all agree we need to update some of these bills. We just started to find things. People came before this committee such as the police who wanted a change in this bill. The sentence for murder was too lax or too great. We can understand that.
It opened up a whole bunch of other things to which people were responding. I certainly do not want to end on a negative note this week. I want to end on a positive note. I think if there is anything good we have learned it is that we have a lot more work to do. Let us not just have a PR campaign. Let us have a real campaign on terms of Canadian security and justice.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make one more point. I would like to ask the hon. member for his opinion.
The parliamentary secretary referred to 24 and 25-year-olds being in youth institutions. The parliamentary secretary knows that need not be the case. It was in his own amendment that while they are waiting for resolution of the question as to which court, adult or youth, they are tried in when they reach 20 they automatically go to an adult court. This is fine. In most of the cases young offenders will serve their term before they are 20. The ones that do not will at least have the opportunity of rehabilitation and training. They need not be 24 or 25. I personally feel that up to 20 is fine.
I would like to know the feeling of the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam on that.

Mr. Speaker, these are the amendments that were introduced at the last moment. I said the other day that I congratulated the government for bringing it in line with what the Prime Minister said at the United Nations.
You are not going to have 25, 26 or 27-year-olds in this situation. It seems to me that the principle is that they are sentenced as a juvenile and treated as a juvenile and then they are kept apart so they do not go in the school for crime. They finish out their sentences.
Then the public, someone like Mr. Rose or others, says that they did get a decent sentence and they did get punished. The victims feel that justice has been done. They do not, as Mr. Rose says, pound the courtroom desk with a hand after the sentence. We give justice as far as possible to some of the victims and families of victims. At the same time we hit the young offenders but
Government Orders
we do not put them in a school for crime. I think that is what was developing in the committee and that is what the hon. member was talking about in the institute.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on Bill C-12, an act to amend the Young Offenders Act and the Criminal Code.
During the last campaign the Young Offenders Act was one of the issues in my particular riding. It was an issue because we have an awful lot of drug related crime in my community. The police consider my particular riding in downtown Toronto to be one of the worst ridings in Canada for crimes relating to drugs. Most of those crimes are committed by young offenders.
I would walk the streets in Broadview-Greenwood and listen to the constituents and also listen to the police forces. Time and time again they said that one of the difficult problems that they have when they are dealing with young offenders is that the rehabilitation process is voluntary rather than mandatory. I campaigned in the last election that if this bill came before the House I would fight for an amendment to this act. The specific amendment would be that the rehabilitation process for crimes by young offenders with drugs would be absolutely mandatory.
As we debate this bill today that is just one of the many amendments that are not in this bill and certainly do not meet that test.
But I want to pick up on something that was said earlier by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice. He said that as we were processing this bill through first reading, second reading and report stage we consulted with the Canadian Bar Association and the police association, et cetera. It seems to me that with this government the word consult is almost like a buzzword. It consulted people on the goods and services tax. It consulted people through the Spicer commission and it is consulting people now on national unity. The minister of trade announced two weeks ago that he was going to be consulting people on competitiveness and prosperity.
If you reflect on this government's consultation process you would almost think that this is one of the most open and consultative governments that we have had around here in many years. But when you strip away the veil of this consultation process you discover that very rarely does this government listen to what the consultants are saying.

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
When I go home on the weekend and listen to my constituents it seems that what they are telling me, whatever the issue, is totally different from what the government consultants are saying. This particular bill on the young offenders is just another example.
The parliamentary secretary said here this morning: "We have consulted". He did mention the police forces. I consulted as well with the metropolitan Toronto police force. On a bill like this I naturally called Police Chief William McCormack last week. His staff superintendent Grant Waddell responded. He wrote the following letter regarding the Young Offenders Act. He wanted his input to be amendments to this bill and I am going to be very specific. Here are the recommendations from the metropolitan Toronto police chief's office.
Recommendation No. 1 was publication of wanted youth. If a young person has committed an indictable offence or is alleged to have committed one there is reason to believe that the young person is dangerous to others. Publication of his name and description is necessary to apprehend him.
Such notice of publication should be in effect until he is apprehended. At the present time it is only in effect for 48 hours.
This is my exercise of consultation and I say this with respect to the parliamentary secretary.
The admissibility of statements taken from young offenders is such a contentious issue that it is felt a distinct new caution should be written into the Young Offenders Act along with guidelines so that each police force deals with it exactly the same.
This way there could be no misunderstanding and the judges could accept them. Distinct rights to counsel should be included in this caution as well as the secondary caution.
Judges should be appointed as youth court judges and deal slowly with young offenders' matters. At the present time family court judges sit as youth court judges. They are dealing with family matters one day and criminal matters the next.
The fourth recommendation concerns sentencing. The maximum sentence a young person can receive is three
years, that is if he is convicted for a crime for which an adult could receive life imprisonment, i.e. murder.
For any other offences the maximum is two years. These maximum sentences should be increased to five years less a day for the most serious. It should be three or four years for crimes involving violence and two years for less serious offences. The five years less a day would still eliminate jury trials. Also at the present time youth can only receive a concurrent sentence. Repeat offenders should receive consecutive sentences.
For youths under 16 years mandatory treatment should be implemented on recommendation from the court's psychiatric assessments. At the present time children can refuse any type of psychiatric treatment after they are convicted. Children 12 to 15 years are not always capable of knowing what treatment is needed or required to benefit them.
An adult over 18 years charged and convicted of an offence committed when he was a young offender serves his time in a young offender's facility. Theoretically a 20-year old adult could serve three years in a facility with 16-year-olds. Anyone over 18 years convicted of an offence under the Young Offenders Act should serve their time in an adult minimum security facility.
Presently a youth sentenced to secure custody can be transferred to open custody by the administrator of the facility. This should only occur if the youth has received some form of treatment and is progressing satisfactorily.
At the present time the young offender's criminal record, not stayed or withdrawn, is kept on file for five years. This should be increased to at least seven years for the purpose of sentencing if he continues his criminal career as an adult.
These are recommendations from the metropolitan Toronto police force.
We talk about consultation. It seems to me that if we are really serious and really committed to drafting legislation that is more than just a public relations gesture, if we take the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice's words sincerely, when he said this morning: "This law passed the test of protection of the public", if we are really sincere about that, how can we then ignore the advice of one of the finest police forces in the world?

November 8, 1991

These are men and women who deal with young offenders day in and day out. It is like asking a carpenter to build a home and not giving him any tools.
How do you expect the people on the street to enforce our laws? How do you expect them to stay committed? How do you expect the reputation for law and order in this country to be maintained when we are ignoring the very enforcers?
Let us talk about our judicial system. Our courts, as the Liberal Party justice critic, the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys, said earlier today are so backlogged right now, our system is so jammed up that we have just finished cancelling 50,000 cases. He gave the example of the young 14-year old girl who was raped by six young offenders and they got off scot-free.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On a point of order. I would not normally interrupt the hon. member but he should know that the case is presently under appeal. As a result I do not think he would want to be referring to any of the details of that case.
I am sure the hon. member would understand that advice.

I take the point but we have been talking about this case all day. However there are similar cases that we all know and have heard about. That is the travesty of our system in Canada today. We do not have enough judges in the system. We do not have enough correctional centres. We do not have a separate system for young offenders in this country and yet we expect our police forces to do a good job. It just does not add up.
We in the Liberal Party are not supporting this legislation. There are several areas of concern. There is no allowance for rehabilitation training. There is no commitment that young offenders will be incarcerated separately from adults. There is no allowance for the establishment of a separate juvenile justice system.
I want to remind the House of the speech made by my colleague from York South-Weston earlier this week, on Monday morning. He stood up in this House and said: "This justice week is a scam. It is a public relations exercise. It is all tactics. It has no substance". We had an opportunity to address a very important piece of legislation to every region of this country. This Young Offenders Act is something that people in Canada are concerned about.
Government Orders
They send us here as legislators to craft legislation, not for tactical reasons but for substantial reasons. In terms of substance this bill does not pass the test of making protection of the public paramount. Those are not my words. They are the words of members of the metropolitan Toronto police force. We have consulted with them. We have listened to them. When you consult with people day in and day out and come back to Ottawa and do not listen to them they begin to wonder what is the point of being consulted if their advice is never taken.
The problem we have in this country right now is that this government has abused and destroyed the consultative process with Canadians. It has set up programs or commissions on issue after issue: the GST, the Spicer commission, the national unity commission and now we are about to get this prosperity and competitiveness consultation process. When you set up these programs and then do not listen to the advice or do listen but do not act upon the advice, what happens? The trust breaks down. We are seeing this trust break down with this government's consultative process right now. We saw it break down on the GST. We see that it is breaking down on national unity. God forbid, no one in this country wants it to break down. The same thing is going to happen on the Minister for International Trade's prosperity and competitive consultative process.
Here on a very important issue, young offenders, a very important piece of legislation, the government said it consulted, but it did not listen. It did not act in a substantive way on any of the advice, or veiy little of the advice that it was given.
As a result we in this party are not going to support this legislation. We are asking the government to withdraw it, come to its senses, start to rebuild some trust in this institution, realize that it is more than just a PR scam, it is more than just a tactical operation, it is more than a public relation show. Let us put some trust back into the system, and withdraw this bill.
I beg the government to listen to tne metropolitan Toronto police force. Give the men and women who walk the streets in my town the tools to do their job. Give the judges and the court system the tools to do their job so that we can make these streets clean again, not just in my city but in every other part of this country.

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
