speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was speaking about the subject of consultation. I would like to point out to the House that it was precisely because people were telling us, including police, police associations and those who work with the juvenile justice and the criminal justice system, that some improvements could be made on the transfer provisions of youth from the youth system to the adult system. It was as a result of that consultation that we made clear in this bill that where the interests of keeping the youth in the system cannot be reconciled with the best interest of the public the interest of the public would prevail on the transfer.
I just have a simple question for the hon. member. What did Chief McCormack say specifically on the transfer provisions? As the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam pointed out, this is not a rewriting of the Young Offenders Act. This is an improvement in certain areas of the Young Offenders Act. More will come. I have indicated to this House that I know it will receive the enthusiastic support from the Liberal Party and others as has our justice legislation this week.
Be that at is may, what did Chief McCormack have to say about the transfer provisions? I would like to ask the hon. member this as well. Will he follow the parliamentary tradition of, having once quoted from a document as he has quite extensively, tabling the document with the Chair?

Mr. Speaker, first of all as I mentioned earlier in my remarks this correspondence from the desk of the police chief, and I mentioned it was signed by Staff Superintendent Grant Waddell, I will be happy to submit to the table.
On the actual transfers, this specific piece of advice that I received from the metropolitan Toronto police force does not address that specifically.
It is a big gap.

The member says it is a big gap. I did say in my remarks that there were some things in this legislation. That does not change my mind at all. Just because there are one or two good things in the legislation, that is no reason to let the legislation go through. Also, the government is already talking about phase two of this legislation. Why enshrine legislation now if you are already admitting that it needs repair? Why not pull it back, fix it, listen, put the amendments in there so that we can all get behind the legislation?
The member smiles. I naturally defer to my justice critic, the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys. It seems to me, if I understood his remarks, that if the bill were to address these substantive changes, these amendments, we in this party are not adverse to supporting the government on this legislation.
My goodness, just this week we see that the gun control legislation is illusory. It is not what the Minister of Justice said it was this morning on Canada AM.
I must give this government credit for one thing. On tactics it gets 10 out 10, but on substance, I will not even make the judgment. I will let the people of Canada judge. I believe that if this bill was withdrawn and we put some of these substantive changes in here the metropolitan Toronto police force is recommending-and I am sure it has had these discussions with many other police associations across Canada-then we on this side of the House would feel a lot better and we would probably get behind it. Is that not what the people of Canada want right now? Do they not want us to get involved in crafting legislation where we can somehow galvanize this country, where we can come together?
November 8, 1991

I see the critic for the New Democratic Party nodding his head in concurrence. Let us get a substantial piece of legislation crafted here so that people can be proud of this House again, rather than put through something that is nothing more than a public relations gesture.

Mr. Speaker, one of the things that is so important in the whole field of corrections is if the police, the court process, the prison system, the conditional release system tie together as a whole to push one part and not deal with the others, you might as well forget it.
The bill today is a public relations exercise that will be accepted. I wonder if the previous speaker would agree that correctional facilities to which these young people are charged in Canada do not protect society and they do not correct offenders. Anyone who survives a prison experience and does not become a recidivist should never have gone in the first place. There were far better and more effective mechanisms to deal with them.
Prisons are one of the unsafest places in the world. I happened to work in one while I was going through university for three years, as a correction and security officer. There is no law in a jail. You do not catch these people, but there are sexual assaults, physical assaults, robbery, extortion and it is one of the most violent, unlawful, unsafe places in the world. When anyone goes there, their life is in jeopardy from the time they go in until the time they come out.
It destroys any positive values of persons who go to the institution because they join with a group of people who believe they are wrongly there. They have no contact with the consequences of their offence and the victims. They usually go there because they have no societal support system. Their only support system is their fellow inmates with a value system that is absolutely wrong, one that they quickly learn.
These people who go to jails go because they have no family, no positive social supports. They are in serious jeopardy of becoming worse instead of better.
The government's restraint program involves staff cuts, failure to provide professional support systems in jails. You do not get psychiatric treatment in any effective way. You do not get counselling in any effective way. You do not get treatment and you do not get corrected.
Government Orders
Working staff ratios in prisons of correctional officer to inmate run 100 to one if you are lucky. As a working correctional officer, I needed the inmates to run the units I ran. If I did not use the inmates, the whole unit turned on me because those inmate leaders who committed the assaults, who did the robbing and extorting, then turned the other 100 inmates on me, and every other correctional officer is in exactly the same position. Therefore you let the offenders and the others run the institution. If you did not, you would not run it.
Staff need inmates to run those institutions. There are not enough of them to do it effectively themselves. Staff, police and correctional officers develop a disease which I call "scum of the earthitis". You had to believe that the people you were dealing with were the scum of the earth in order to do some of the things that were done to them.
Basically, because of the restraint programs of this government and because of single public relations exercises, this is bound to failure. This does not address the needs of the entire system to protect society and reform offenders. Would the member agree?

Mr. Speaker, I will give a short answer.
Here is a perfect example of where this House of Commons is just upside down. No wonder people consider this place irrelevant. I am not a lawyer. I am a small businessman who happened to get lucky because he knocked on a few doors and listened to people.
Here is a member of Parliament who has probably had more experience in working with the correctional service system than anyone else in this House. How can we not listen to his point of view? We do not need to go out, hire consultants and spend millions of dollars. I can only agree with the hon. member. I think his experience, his observations and his recommendations should be plugged right into the amendments of this act.
That is the kind of thing that would make this legislation something of substance.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments on this bill. I have had some experience in the correctional system in Canada, and as a result of it through the conditional release system and the police system in which the three are an organic whole along with the courts.

November 8, 1991
Government Orders
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca and my brother from Comox-Albemi have also worked in the correctional system and do have a good broad base in it.
The point I would like to make is that the Young Offenders Act deals with murder. I think my colleague overstates the case when he says it deals with one-fortieth of one per cent. It is probably not even that high.
Given the absolutely small, narrow scope of this bill, it is a real tragedy. In every community I represent, property offences are rampant. They are absolutely rampant. They break into businesses and steal all kinds of goods. They break into homes and steal. They break into automobiles, and it is just of epidemic proportion.
What is happening is that we do not have enough police. We do not have enough public consciousness in those communities to stop them. The most rampant offences are property offences.
In one of the communities in discussing with the RCMP the matter, it said that if we could remove six young people from the system who we know are doing it, we could end half the property offences in the community: six young people.
He said that they are all repeat offenders, and he said: "We know exactly who they are, but catching them is a terrible problem. Not only that, once we have them, dealing with them is even worse of a problem".
This bill does not protect citizens from crime. It increases a penalty for murder. Once they go to a correctional facility, society is not protected because they come out. They still do not have the support systems and there is no effective treatment. The chance for repetition is certainly there.
It misses the mark because of the epidemic proportion of property crimes, the fact that police know who the offenders are and we in this Parliament have hamstrung their ability to deal with them. We have to correct that and stop this nonsense about PR.
I had the occasion to sit on a family court committee in Courtenay, B.C. for a period. I chaired it for a while. The
judge who dealt with it was an individual who was sentencing young people to what he thought was an institution that unfortunately had been closed years before. When it was pointed out to him that he was sending them to an adult institution, he was shocked. He had thought it was for young people, and in fact he was sending these young offenders to an adult institution.
I am sceptical that judges have enough background. They tend to rely quickly on things like incarceration of offenders. I think there is the matter of education and experience of judges with the correctional system. That is sorely needed. It does not protect society. Those people come before them again and again. But we do not place very much in the hands of the courts either in terms of flexibility.
I think we have to look hard at the tools we provide the courts with. Definitely prison sentencing has to be there. I am one who believes that in an appropriate institution we should probably sentence people to the maximum sentence possible. The judge may have an opportunity to state the minimum time that the person should spend there, but also the maximum, and we should make it very easy for conditional release.
Under conditional release the person finds a sponsor who will support them to return to the community, because so many of the people who go to jail have no social support system other than other offenders. Their parental control has fallen apart. The school control system has fallen apart and their friends, their source of values, their source of incentive wind up being other offenders. That is a serious problem.
An offender who goes to jail must have the responsibility of planning a conditional release program. The person has to take responsibility for that. The longer the sentence, the more incentive there is going to be to plan an acceptable release program.
An offender needs a sponsor, somebody who has the general acceptance of the community. The old Borstal system in English that was transferred into some areas of Canada had the most successful recovery rate for offenders because it did rely on a sponsor system. The sponsor
November 8, 1991

Government Orders
and the inmate worked out the conditional release program. It involved employment, education, where to live, who the contacts would be, and a gradual step by step process by which the person had a very positive individual to work with. That kind of a commitment on the part of an offender to find a sponsor, somebody who will befriend them, assist them, and to work out an acceptable release program is certainly going to be a positive move forward in helping that offender not to repeat again.
Before a person goes to jail, compensation and restitution have to be part of the system. The offender must confront the victim, if it is acceptable on the part of the victim, and there has to be some form of compensation and restitution. It certainly deals a lot more heavily with the offender, the consequences of the offence, and it is an absolutely important thing.
In terms of giving the court tools, longer sentences where there is a much easier opportunity for acceptable conditional release would be a very positive move. Offenders who decide they do not want to become involved in working out pre-release arrangements that are acceptable certainly will spend a longer period of time in there and will be exposed to treatment over a longer period of time, and there is an incentive to change.
What appears to occur in correctional institutions is that those who are convicted and have short sentences say: "I would rather serve my full sentence and avoid conditions when I leave, rather than get tied up in a parole system and long conditional releases". It is not in the interest of society to have that happen. It is not in the interest of society not to have offenders appreciate the full nature and consequences of the act they have done by being able to avoid the victim in the situation.
I have already made my remarks about the correctional system, and I would like to repeat them in part. Correctional institutions do not protect society because offenders are released. They do not correct offenders because they are not provided with enough money by the government, this government or previous governments. Some of the lowest salaries, I would assume, in the government are probably paid to correctional workers. Staff training and the ability to obtain professional help in the form of psychiatrists, counsellors and others generally are very limited.
If we are going to deal with young offenders, we have to address the court system. We have to address the number of police. We have to address programs within the society. We also have to put some support into the correctional system and demand from the correctional system some accountability in making sure that the recidivism rate drops. If it does not they are not doing it correctly. If we do not provide them with the resources it is not happening correctly.
They are the unsafest places in the world. We cannot guarantee the safety of an inmate. I had an experience of travelling through the unit one morning after working night shift and finding an individual who had his head severely pounded by his fellow inmates who decided to put rocks in a sock and beat the can off the individual. There are hundreds and hundreds of these stories where somebody goes into a stairwell and does not come out the other end. They have either received a knife or a terrible beating because of some problem.
We cannot guarantee safety. One night in the institution on parade, as we were getting a briefing on the circumstances, the sergeant in charge said: "There are 100 knives missing from the kitchen tonight. The institution is not upset. It does not feel upset, but there are 100 knives floating around in there". It was an interesting shift. There is no way of guaranteeing the protection of the people who are confined there.
The value system is very important. Everybody serving time in jail believes they are there on what is called a bum, that they have been placed there incorrectly and improperly, that they were not responsible for what happened. Every other person is convinced of that. It is the easy road to believe. The accountability of anyone who goes there diminishes and it is the other side's responsibility. That is a very unhealthy thing to happen in terms of correcting an offender.
Again talking to staff is a punishable offence in the inmate community, so you do not befriend staff members who are working with ratios of 100 to 1. You do not communicate in any confidential way with staff members. Your confidants, your communicators and your people who set your value system for a number of years are the other offenders of the institution. It is an extremely unhealthy situation.

Government Orders
There needs to be far greater flexibility in terms of conditional release. When inmates are ready to go they should be released immediately. Maybe the prison administrators need more authority. Then when persons have worked out a conditional release arrangement, have found a sponsor, have found a training program and an acceptable set of conditions to go back to society and try to make, they should not have to wait for an extended parole board operation. Inmates held up for three to six months. Once the program is in place there should be a way of letting them out to try a fast tracking of the arrangement.
Those things are coming into place but when they get out there, there seems to be very little effective supervision. If we limit the number in a restraint program of probation officers, if we do not involve parents and sponsors effectively, we are not going to be successful because they are going to gravitate back to their friends who have been released from the institution and the people who got them into difficulty in the beginning. The cycle will begin again.
The failure to provide adequate supervision and adequate resources after release or while on conditional release certainly mitigates against protecting society, correcting an offender, and brings us right back into the cycle again.
The Young Offenders Act changes today are just a very small window dressing aspect of this entire problem. It would be useful I think to very frustrated police forces in Canada if the recommendations of the member for Broadview-Greenwood were incorporated and if a great deal more attention was given by this Elouse to placing in the hands of the courts more flexibility in sentencing and to more resources for the institutions that treat these people so that they can protect their lives while they are in there, that we do not see a massive erosion in their value system and that they can effectively plan a conditional release program.
The probation and parole supervision system should be supported with enough people and enough resources so that when offenders are released on conditional release there is half a fighting chance that they can get out in society and correct their behaviour.
It is a subject of long-standing frustration. It is not a
matter of a bleeding heart. I believe offenders should be forced to face the consequences of their act fully, that they should be required to make restitution and compensation to victims. We should provide the resources and the incentives for them to return to society and work at self-correction.
One of the areas where we are missing an opportunity is that of much longer sentences. If an offender refuses to work out an acceptable conditional release program and refuses to work to develop the support in society that will make them positive citizens then they will have to stay in the institution until they are prepared to do so.

Madam Speaker, I listened very carefully to the comments of the hon. member because he referred us to his own personal experiences. I am sure I am not the only one who was dismayed to hear about the conditions in prisons that the hon. member has personally experienced. That is a great tragedy and I think most Canadians would be extremely disheartened to learn that there appears to be no order in the prisons of today.
I do not want to talk about prisons. I want to talk about young offenders. My question is addressed to the member based on his experiences.
I gather that the point the member was making is that: "You cannot guarantee the safety of an inmate because of their own law within the prison". We are certainly in agreement that young offenders should not be placed in an environment like that.
If we have correctional facilities set apart for young offenders would it not be the same sort of law and the same type of behaviour, only with younger people? What sort of protection could be offered in that kind of facility to ensure that those young offenders in a correctional facility devoted solely to them would not in fact become merely a younger mirror image of the place where the hon. member worked?
I hope the hon. member will have constructive comments on that.

Madam Speaker, the correctional institution at Haney was in its day one of the leading institutions in Canada. The first warden of the place is probably still kicking around in the federal correctional system.
November 8, 1991

It aimed at treatment of offenders from age 14 to 25. The oldest individual was 25. At one point we had somebody who was 40 and was very carefully selected before being allowed to go there. It usually involved special training and education.
Most of the crime in society is committed by younger people. Some of the worst crimes that I have ever heard of, or had the misfortune to open the folders on, were committed by teenagers who wound up in that institution. Those people were responsible for the most violent assaults; they had that kind of value system. Clifford Olson was an inmate of that institution. For 10 years afterwards I read in the paper of people who came out of there and promptly went into the B.C. penitentiary, having murdered people and committed all sorts of offences.
At the beginning it was a school for the penitentiary. There were incredible tragedies in the place. It was basically young offenders inflicting the kinds of things I was talking about on other young offenders.
The failure in the place was the staff to inmate ratio. You cannot do anything when you are dealing with 500 inmates. On an afternoon or night shift after program we were looking at eight staff for 500 inmates. I can remember being left in the movie theatre with seven other colleagues and 500 inmates. There were not enough staff to cover the lights and the projection room. We were locked in and there were four other staff and the administrator outside patrolling the outside areas. When the order in the dark broke down there were eight of us and 500 inmates.
I was under the impression that they were going to be peeling us off the wall by the time the RCMP finally got in and broke it up. When you are dealing with effective working staff ratios of 100 to 1 you cannot do anything effective. In many cases you need the leaders of the unit to assist you in keeping it running. That is a common technique staff use to survive.

Madam Speaker, I want to ask the hon. member a question. I listened to his speech and I was very impressed, particularly with the fact that he has actually gone through it. It was not second hand or third hand. He has actually experienced it. It was quite informative.
Government Orders
I wanted him to reiterate whether he thought, particularly with respect to young people, there is any rehabilitative function at all in prison if they do not get organized rehabilitation and counselling from properly trained officials. Is there any rehabilitative nature in prisons at all?

Over a three-year period it dealt with a very large number of people. One of the most violent people I have ever known was one of the hardest workers. He was one of the most respectable individuals but under a stress condition he lost it. He was about 18 years old, a very large strapping guy. The chance that he would go out and kill somebody was very high. He was in for an auto theft on a very short sentence. He was a problem that was going to create a problem for society but nobody could do anything. It was like having a bomb going out on to the street.
Six people were drunk, broke into an A & W, attempted to fry up some hamburgers and were too drunk to accomplish the task. The judge sentenced them to almost 18 months in jail for that offence. The cost to the public was terrible. The destruction of whatever faith they had in the value system was nearly complete. One of them almost killed himself because he developed a habit of sniffing gas.
Rehabilitation is directly related to quickly catching their interest in getting released with an acceptable plan, in trying to develop in a failed family the supports to get that individual out of jail. The faster you can get them out of jail, the better off society is going to be.
I had the impression when I worked there that if we released every single person the crime rate would not go up appreciably.

Like the other members, I found the member's comments from first-hand experience fascinating.
One of the things that twigged my mind was the role of victims. I wondered whether they felt anything toward their victims or whether the victims could be brought into the process. About a month ago when I was coming home I saw a policeman in front of my apartment building and I thought "Oh, no".

I went in and my apartment had been broken into. They had caught the culprit right in the living room, arrested him and took him away. I have never seen him. I heard it was a young man. I do not know who it is. I lost a couple of small things, like my TV. Luckily that is all I lost because they caught him. However they took that away as evidence. I wonder if the hon. member can tell me if he has had any experience in terms of how the inmates feel about their victims, how we could bring the victim into the process and maybe how the police could start talking to the victims.

I have a couple of thoughts. I do not think a short jail sentence particularly bothers a person that has been there before. In Okalla there was a phenomenon around Christmas time when it is cold out on the street and they do not have a square meal if they are poor. So they threw a rock through a window. The first time they would get 30 days, then 60 days and then 90 days. A group of people in Vancouver used to call it "doing life on the instalment plan". It provided them with room and board and a good job and all their old friends.
Going to jail and not confronting the victim almost eases the penalty in some cases for the offender because the personal problem of having to confront a victim in some cases is more threatening, more guilt generating than going to jail.
In the area I represent just recently two people spent 30 and 60 days in jail for some nasty property offences. They got out and it became a badge in the rest of the community for them to say "I have been to jail". It enhances their status and prestige. Confronting the victims and being forced to discuss the nature of the offence and what would be appropriate restitution could be far more threatening than a short period of incarceration.

Madam Speaker, I would like to start by thanking my colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys for giving me this opportunity to
speak on Bill C-12, the proposed amendment to the Young Offenders Act.
The bill focuses mainly on, first, easing the criteria under which applications for transfer to adult court are to be judged by the youth court. For example, transfer would be more easily obtained.
Second, it would increase the maximum period of incarceration for first and second degree murder from three years to five years less a day. This would eliminate the need for jury trial.
Third, for the first time the youth court could deal with parole eligibility and could set the conditions for conditional supervision for those charged with murder.
Looking at those points, there seems to be a shift away from treatment and rehabilitation to protection of society or enforcement of the law.
The reason I wanted to speak on this bill is twofold. First, there is the question of the United Nations resolution on the rights of the child. Canada's role in fulfilling its commitment, in particular section 37(c) of the charter, would not be fulfilled unless Canada guarantees a separate facility for youths and adults.
Somewhere in this bill the government has to make sure that the criteria are met. It is my belief that the government will come up with a reservation on this particular point. Looking at the Young Offenders Act it does not seem to be evident to me that the government will be able to fulfil its commitment.
It is my hope that whatever those reservations are the government will proceed with the ratifying the charter and will fulfil its commitment internationally.
The latest Statistics Canada report, which was published in the spring of 1991, indicates that youths between the ages of 12 and 17 were responsible for nearly 25 per cent of all Criminal Code offences, as violent crime in Canada reached an all-time high. Nationally the 1991 violent crime rate is about 1,012 offences per 100,000 population, which is the highest in the history of Canada.
Approximately 20,000 more violent crimes were committed this year over last year. For instance, British Columbia, which had the highest rate, had approximately
15,000	incidents per 100,000 population. Ontario had approximately 9,500 per 100,000. That is quite alarming.

As my previous colleague indicated, the property crime rate rose by about 7 per cent last year to approximately 5,869 incidents per 100,000 population.
If you look at the total number of incidents or the total number of people who got in trouble, youths between the ages of 12 and 17, in 1990-91 there were 38,000 defendants that age who appeared in youth court.
They faced approximately 118,000 charges. That is approximately 4 per cent over the last year. If you look at the population in Canada, the youth between the ages of 12 and 17, we have close to 1.125 million. Females, we have approximately 1,069,500. This is a total of approximately 2.195 million males and females between the ages of 12 and 17.
Thirty-eight thousand is quite a number of people who get in trouble. If you look at the crimes that were committed, charges have risen by 20 per cent over the past five years while the majority of those were committed in property crimes. Fifty-eight per cent of all charges relate to properties.
The rest of the crimes involve breaches of probation orders, drug offences and a variety of miscellaneous offences. The sad thing about this whole situation is that 70 per cent of those cases produced a guilty verdict with probation.
The most common sentence in a jail or a half-way house is only 25 per cent of those cases. While this is an interesting statistic, it is my suggestion that jail is not doing the job. I will remind you of a study which was done by Professor Handleby who looked at the province of Ontario.
He said that in the first study ever of its kind, actually 17 years survey of males first incarcerated under the Ontario training system, there was a 90 per cent failure rate. It is a 90 per cent failure rate.
Among the 150 young inmates originally interviewed in 1970 when they were aged 12 to 14, only 9 per cent incurred no subsequent conviction, according to Mr. Handleby. He is saying that in fact in 1987, when he did the tracking of 97 per cent of those original groups, he learned that they had accumulated in excess of 2,261 convictions since they turned 16. This is an average of more than 15 each, ranging from drug possession to murder.

In fact, 48 per cent of the original 150 or 72 individuals had committed violent crimes. In general, the survey concluded that the earlier the age at which the youth breaks the law, the more likely he will go on to offend again. That was the result of the finding.
It looked like dealing with the problem after it occurred. It does not seem to address the question at hand and does not seem to be producing the solutions we are interested in.
What I think is extremely important for us is to look at the people we are dealing with to see who they are and where they are coming from. According to information which we were able to obtain from the province of Ontario, the ministry of social services looked at the profile of kids who get in trouble. They were able to identify 12 characteristics which I would like to share with you, Madam Speaker, and with Canadians.
The first characteristic of a young offender is that he or she will come from a lower class origin. In fact, 65 per cent of parents of kids who get in trouble have less than grade 10 education.
The second one is they look at problems in the family of origin, for example, long-term reliance on welfare; criminality in family of origin, for example the parents, siblings, other relatives; multiple psychological handicaps, low verbal intelligence.
Third, the ministry indicates that the profile of kids that get into trouble shows personal temperament, attitude and early behavioural history. They looked at the issue of aggression, restless energy, the impulsive, the adventurous and a taste for taking risk and again, below average verbal intelligence, poor problem solving, coping, self-regulation skills.
Fourth, they indicated early and current family conditions again repeat itself, low level of affection, cohesiveness, low level of supervision and poor discipline, neglect, abuse.
Fifth, which is in my view one of the most important ones, school based risk factors, below average efforts, lack of interest, being bored, not worrying about occupational future, conduct problems.
Sixth, schooling again, personal, educational, vocational, socio-economic achievement and they indicated the low level achieved in education, for adults long periods of unemployment, reliance on welfare.

Government Orders
Seventh, interpersonal relationships, generalized indifference to opinion of others, weak effective ties, for adults an unstable marital history.
Eighth, companions, association with anti-social, drug using others, isolation from non-criminal others.
Ninth, personal attitude, values, belief, feelings.
Tenth, behavioural history, criminal history, juvenile and adults.
Eleventh, psycho-pathology.
Twelfth, other risk factors, being male for instance, being young, 14 to 24 and a variety of other issues.
Just looking at all of those 12 points, there is one thing I think that jumps in front of everybody in this Chamber. There is one leading factor, that most of those kids are coming from a low income family, where the family's education is less than grade 10, 65 per cent of them. Those kids are not going to school. In every single one of these 12 elements, directly and indirectly, one would conclude without question that lack of education is the leading cause of the fact that we have the situation we are in right now with young offenders.
That is why in our society rather than all the time dealing with the problem itself, we have to try to find a solution to the problem and go right to the source. It is fine if I have a headache and I take an aspirin, but I think it is far more important for me to deal with the problem at the source in preventing the headache.
That would lead me to some of the examples in my community, what the people who are enforcing the law are doing at the same time. I am going to take the example of the Ottawa police force under the leadership of Chief Tom Flanagan. It has embarked on a most magnificent ventures, that is crime prevention as it relates to youth.
In May 1990 the Ottawa police force established a youth centre. The youth centre was established to provide a facility where area youths could participate in activities supervised by volunteer police officers. The objective of this was to provide a range of activities that challenged youth of all ages and to provide a safe recreational environment that encourages team work and enjoyment, to encourage local residents and nonpolice volunteers to participate and promote a better understanding between youth and police.
You may ask if this is the role of the police force, to be involved in recreational activities. Well, just hang on. The initial start-up fund for this particular centre was received from the city of Ottawa, the Ottawa Police Commission, service clubs, which is the private sector, and various concerned members of the community. The centre is located in a renovated old fire station provided free of charge by the city of Ottawa at 1463 Prince of Wales at the comer of Meadowlands Drive. This location, and this is the most important point of this whole debate, was chosen because of its close proximity to a housing project, an area with a long history of police enforcement. It is hoped that this police initiative will allow area youth to relate to police members in a positive environment.
Some of the things that the youths in that area will do at the centre is play volleyball, basketball, ball hockey, broomball, football, soccer, boxing, weight-lifting, table tennis, pool, and various social activities are also available such as field trips, movie nights and dances. Many of the youths use the centre on a drop-in basis to meet their friends and, more important than anything, as a hanging out centre.
In this area, approximately 150 youths, predominantly male between the age of 7 to 16, attend on a regular basis with 50 every day on the average, every evening, and approximately 90 per cent of them live in the surrounding area.
The Ottawa police looked at the geography and demography of the area and set up a centre in order to recruit kids to come to that centre so it would be a joint venture between the Ottawa police force and the community so they can create some sort of an environment for these kids to go and hang out.
In this centre they have two paid positions. Funding is provided, in some cases, by local businesses and they have many off-duty police officers. We also have a community college which is involved with the police force. Constable Brian Edge of our Ottawa police force is the police liaison officer for the youth centre and oversees the facility. He reports to Bruce Harrison who is in charge of this department.
The reason why I want to give this example is to tell you how proud I am of members of our police force not only looking at the letter of the law, but by going beyond the call of duty and recognizing, because they are like my

colleague from the other side of the House, the need for preventive measures before the problem occurs. They do this on their own time and at their own expense, giving unselfishly so that they can deal with the problem.
Why can they not spend more? The funding is the question which my colleague from Cape Breton and my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood spoke about many, many times, saying that funding is a key question when it comes to preventive measures.
There is one segment which is extremely important and which I have an interest in. We as a society do not recognize the magnitude of the problem when it comes to our youth. Here are some shocking statistics. A Senate committee published a report indicating that over the next 20 years approximately 187,000 children will quit school because of the effect of no money at home. For the purpose of this analysis consider them simply as an economic unit which will affect our national well-being for good or bad.
The report goes on and is bad, as it turns out. These
187,000	dropouts will cost the federal and provincial treasuries about $7.2 billion in income tax.
In addition they will cost the rest of us another $1.15 billion in foregone consumption taxes such as the terrible GST. Our society will lose $220 million in reduced unemployment insurance contributions as a result of poverty shaping these units. Furthermore, it will cost us $660 million in increased unemployment insurance cheques and another $710 million in extra welfare bills.
I am going to move on very quickly and tell the House that Canada's Gross National Product will be cut by an estimated $23 billion in lost income from these 187,000 unproductive units, these 187,000 kids who are leaving school. The total national bill for these poverty induced dropouts will come to $33 billion.
Here is the conclusion. The report argues that spending $5 billion over those 20 years on things like classroom assistants, child and youth workers, other skilled people, hot lunch programs and proven techniques to build the self-esteem of low income children could erase that $33 billion cost.
Imagine, a $33 billion return on an investment of $5 billion over 20 years. That is better than the best of blue

chips. For a nation that is already overspending at the rate of $30 billion a year and that has a national debt rapidly approach $400 billion, surely we could spend the $5 billion to deal effectively with the incredible question of illiteracy and dropouts in our society.

Something I might like to add is that it could be my child or your child. It is not necessarily always somebody else's child and it is not necessarily somebody from a low income family.
If I could relate back to my own riding where the average income is probably slightly higher than the national average, the police service department in our community has had to recognize a very serious problem with our young people. That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing marketing boards, income plans and price guarantees to ensure that income gaps within the farming community are narrowed and to ensure a continued supply of quality foodstuffs at reasonable and stable prices.
He said: Madam Speaker, today I want to discuss some of the background to the farm situation that has been coming before this House quite often. We have been hearing questions for a long time but particularly as the net farm income problem gets worse in this country. I only mention that because it seems to me that while we hear about it an awful lot in Question Period, in Private Members' Business and on opposition days, I am not sure that we always realize the background to the problem.
I am putting this motion before the House so that as private members we can give range to some ideas from all sides of the House to see if we cannot come up with some other solutions to the so-called income problem.
I do not think we have to spend too much time convincing ourselves that there is in fact an income problem. The projections for the 1991 calendar year project net farms income of just over $3.75 billion. That is down from the actual figures in 1989 of $4.8 billion. In 1988 we had $3.6 billion. In 1987 we had $4.1 billion. In 1986 we had $4.4 billion.
In other words that is six years of barely adequate incomes. We have had a great many bankruptcies and communities feeling extreme financial stress during those years from 1986 to 1991. Yet this year's projected net farm income, after all government programs have been factored in, is expected to be about $3.27 billion, down from almost $5 billion just two years ago. Of this projected $3.27 billion, $2.9 billion of that comes from government payments, which leaves less than $500 million arrived at from the market. So we begin to see, I hope, that there is a real problem out there. The answer is not simply for government to leave farmers to their own devices and sign a free trade arrangement at the GATT where it will swear an agreement that it will no longer provide assistance to farmers. There has to be something more; the over-all problem must be looked at.
The government proposes that a free trade agreement world-wide or with the 107 or 108 countries that are part of the GATT will be the solution. Some academics point out that is not much of a solution. They have done the econometric models with 100 per cent backing away from subsidies and tariffs. They say that world prices of grains and oilseeds will only rise at a maximum of 12 per cent.
Canadian data show the current proposal of 30 per cent reductions might produce an increase of about 4.8 per cent or 5 per cent. This is not enough to make any difference to the net income of Canada's farms.
So what is wrong? Government members are saying that it is a trade war. It is all Europe's fault. Other members in the House point out that the U.S. actions are not exactly Simon Pure either. We have to recognize that Canada has been caught up in responding to a lot of the same political realities that the Europeans and the Americans have put forward.
November 8, 1991

It seems to me that we are playing with a problem and a misunderstanding of agriculture that have been haunting this sector for many years. Agriculture has only been in existence on this planet for probably 5,000 or 6,000 years. Before that civilizations developed as hunter-gatherer societies. They let nature do the production and the people gathered the crops that were produced.
It was not until about 5,000 or 6,000 years ago that people began intervening and planting the seeds, growing the crops and cultivating them.
Why is it important? In Canada's economy it is extremely important because between 23 and 24 per cent of our Gross National Product has its beginnings in agriculture. Almost 24 per cent of the people who are employed in our economy would not be there if there was no food to process or transport or produce or retail or wholesale. Almost 24 per cent of the jobs in this country would not exist if we stopped producing our own food. We could probably handle imported food with 4 per cent or 5 per cent of the labour force as long as we could trust the supplies from all around the globe. We do not need to be rocket scientists or very clever economists to understand that the price of those imported foodstuffs would be much higher than they would be grown close to home.
All of this 25 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product is dependent on the production of slightly less than 3 per cent of the population who are farmers. They look after the land and the primary food production in this country.
Why do we get into these difficulties? Every 10 or 15 years we get into this sort of crisis. I think part of it lies in the fact that the industry is badly misunderstood by academics, politicians and business leaders and has been for a long time. We go back to the beginnings of the middle of the age of enlightenment and we have the parlour experts like Malthus who produced a well thought theory that said that as populations increased the world would eventually starve to death. He proved by mathematical formula that the population of people rose in a geometric progression and the ability to increase food production was only arithmetic. This was false. There is nothing in recent history or even back in the 17th and 18th centuries when this was very popular to prove that had any validity.

Farm people have been able to find all sorts of ways of producing surpluses on little spaces of ground where they should not be able to produce surpluses. We only have to look at recent events.
The country of China is the most populous country on the globe. It was considered a half a century ago to be unable to ever produce enough food to sustain the more than a billion people which it has now as a population. They are self-sufficient in food.
They simply changed the way that they did it. They changed some of the priorities of their society. They made the production of food something that was considered a worthy task and they paid accordingly. The food cycle works in that country.
That is an emerging developing country that has been able to do that. Look at some of the highly technical countries like those of the European Economic Community. Two decades ago the EEC was considered to be a food importer forever. It is considered by this country, Australia, New Zealand and the countries that have a low population and big land base with productivity factors for agricultural production, to be a perpetual market for their foodstuffs.
The Europeans noted that there are some big advantages to their own internal economies if they are selfsustaining in food because of the kind of factors that I will be mentioning shortly. If you take a relatively low cost food product and process it and take it through the economic system, you find that its value has increased many times and has provided wages and work and profits for literally hundreds of people.
They saw it as an engine of growth for their economy so they paid their producers very well to produce enough food to make them self-sufficient in the basic foodstuffs. That economy has emerged as one of the power groups on the globe today.
Another power group in the global economy is Japan. It is considered probably the pre-eminent industrial society on the globe today. When you look at the basic economic realities of their agriculture and their agricultural policy you find what for a lot of people is a surprising fact.

November 8, 1991
Private Members' Business
Japan is virtually self-sufficient in the production of food. It produces enough rice to feed itself and to meet its basic needs. Their fishermen can go out to sea and provide enough protein supplement in the form of products from the sea to meet the protein requirements. They have met their basic protein and hydrocarbon necessities within those small islands. As densely populated as they are, they are virtually self-sufficient in food.
Current parlour experts are saying that supply side economics will look after things. If we only have free trade everything will come to a harmonious balance. I think we should be looking again at the advice they are giving. Those nations which have ignored that advice are the nations that are the most profitable, the most prosperous, have the highest living standards and the most likelihood of a good and continuing future.
Why is Canada not looking at some of the examples of the Japanese and the Europeans instead of toying with a new parlour set of economics like supply side economics where we are attempting to let the market determine things by producing an excess of supply in order to keep things going.
One of the difficulties with this whole theory is that it cannot be sustained. The ultimate end of such an economic cycle is a continued downturn in incomes, in living standards and in future prospects.
If you want to see how the policy is affecting farmers you only have to go back and look at the net income figures that I have placed before the House just a moment ago.
The figures put out by Statistics Canada on agriculture show that net farm incomes have been declining consistently for the last six or seven years. That is the result of this kind of a policy.
What would happen if we followed the European or the Japanese example? Let us take a couple of cases. Let us look at something that was raised at one of the farm rallies in Saskatchewan over the last month. One woman stood up and mentioned to the assembled farmers that her family had been very fortunate this year in being able to sell a carload of malting barley for which they will get after all government payments and final payments approximately $8,000. This is for about 3,500 bushels of barley.
That barley when turned into beer, which is what it is going to be used for, will produce 1.3 million glasses of beer. The taxation revenue from that carload of barley or those 1.3 million glasses of beer will be just over $200,000. In other words, if the Government of Canada needed another $1 million all it would have to do is process five carloads of barley, which would easily fit in this Chamber. There would be $1 million worth of tax revenue generated but the farmers would get under $40,000 for their effort, for which they paid all of their costs for fertilizer, fuel, land rental and so on. They are not getting enough to have anything left over to feed or raise their families.
Wheat is now selling at $2 a bushel, which means that for a $1 loaf of bread less than 4 cents goes to the farmer. The other 96 cents of that loaf of bread goes to the people who are responsible for the transportation, processing and the packaging. In fact the package costs several times more than what the farmer got for the original wheat.
If that carload of barley generated over $250,000 worth of product, why is it only worth $8,000? What happens to the economy if they decide that they are going to finally have to stop producing the barley and over $500,000 worth of economic activity goes down the drain for want of a few dollars to keep a farmer producing the original product?
The market economy that we live in on a global basis is much more complex than these examples. However I think the House gets the idea about what can be obtained. The very complex societies like the European and the Japanese have fallen on this with a vengeance. They have put it to good use in their societies to keep both people and their social and environmental structures current in their particular landscape.
The reality we have to face in the kind of markets that have developed world-wide is that most of the trade in grain and food products is dominated by multinational corporations. They are pressing very hard for nation states to do away with boundaries and any regulations or controls that will have any effect on their ability to trade between nation states. They want to be completely free of any government control or influence of any type. The
November 8, 1991

free trade agreements being touted around the world right now will permit that.
What does it do to the rural communities, to the farmers, or indeed to those same nation states when such a regime is in place? It means that they have very little bargaining power and there is virtually no prospect for a firm and secure future for those nation states, those communities or those farm people.
We have no method of counteracting the power of these large multinational corporations in the marketplace, many of which have larger gross revenues than the gross domestic products of most of the world's countries.
With this motion I am proposing that we take a more serious look at the establishment of marketing boards and have permissive legislation so that farmers can group together and face these large entities in the marketplace on more equal terms.
I am suggesting that governments should be more cognizant of the role that the food producer plays in providing the basic impetus for the economy, particularly in that one-quarter of the economy is food based.
I am suggesting that some new approaches have to be raised and discussed. Until we change the policy direction this country has been following, rural communities and their farm people cannot survive. We have to look at something like I am proposing in this motion.

Madam Speaker, I just wanted to make a few brief comments with regard to the motion put forward by the member for Mackenzie. I know that he has spent a lot of time studying this issue and certainly relates to it very well. It is important that a number of things be outlined as to what is happening with the government and the agricultural policy in Canada.
As I read the motion the inference is that nothing is really happening. We talk about considering the advisability of establishing marketing boards. Everyone in this room and in the country knows that marketing boards are a very important policy element of this country and this government. In fact, the minister spoke about it earlier today in Question Period when a question was put
Private Members' Business
regarding marketing boards. He stated, quite unequivocally and quite clearly, that government support for supply management had not wavered. That applies not only to this level of government but also to the provincial level of government.
When talking about these issues it is important to understand what the government has been doing. It has been doing a lot of things when it comes to agriculture. I could go on with other things about income plans. If I have time maybe I will try to discuss some of those things.
The government embarked on a very comprehensive review of Canadian agricultural policy. A few months a publication called Growing Together came out. It explained to Canadians what was going on and what the future was for agriculture in Canada. As the member who spoke previously said, agriculture is very important to Canada. It is a very essential industry to the Canadian economy.
We have to develop the industry. We cannot say: Well, because we did this in farming or this in agriculture 50 years ago we can do the same thing today and expect the same kind of results. In most of the fanning community, certainly in the ones in my area, their methods of farming, their methods of agriculture and their productivity levels have changed dramatically in the last number of years, and I commend them for that. Those are the kinds of things which we must address. They are producing different crops today than even five years ago, in many instances. That is the kind of thing our agricultural industry is going to have to examine.
When we talked about Growing Together there were really four pillars. One of them was market responsiveness, so that the agricultural industry could relate to the needs of the Canadian economy and the world economy. The other pillars related to self-reliance in the agrifood industry so that farmers have the ability and capability to manage their own affairs, manage their own business and the tools necessary to do that. The other thing that was a part of that program was to recognize that farms in different parts of the country are different. Different parts of regions within the country are different. That was another aspect of it.

Private Members' Business
The final pillar really was an aspect relating to environmental sustainability. That is a terminology that maybe is a little difficult for us to understand because we think of the agricultural industry as being a very natural industry. It is an industry that is friendly to the environment and in many cases, and probably most cases, it is. There are methods and chemicals today. There are practices that are going on today that are not going to help our environment. I think that is a very major factor. I really commend the agricultural industry for taking that aspect into account when it looks at what it is and how it is addressing the particular industry and that part of the economy.
There have been many actions that have come out of this. Both the federal and provincial governments are working together to have a stronger and healthier agricultural sector and I think that is very, very important.
There have been a number of task forces put together, particularly in the supply management marketing board system and certainly in the dairy and poultry sectors. These groups are looking at different aspects as to just what direction their groups are going to go. They are certainly supplying the kind of support that is necessary to the ministry and to the minister to bring those levels together so that the industry will be stable and the income can be stabilized from within, not from government handouts and from other things. That is the kind of thing that they are doing.
The group that is working with the minister at the provincial level is talking about things like greater participation and accountability, transparency, market responsiveness and competitiveness within the systems. I think that is important to everyone who is involved and certainly it applies to the agricultural industry. It applies to the people who are marketing the products, the people who are consuming the products. A lot of times in these kinds of discussions we kind of forget about the fact that the consumer is a big part of the agricultural industry. It is very important that they get involved.
Another steering committee that has been designed between government and the industry, that is agricultural farmers and the consumers, has put together a committee to review this report and to develop action plans as related to the recommendations in that particular report.
As they make those recommendations, it is obvious that we are going to have to start implementing. We are going to have to bring some of those recommendations to the floor.
If we build on this kind of change, the kind of input from the various sectors that are involved, that is the kind of consensus and the kind of results that are going to be veiy positive for all parts and everyone who is involved in that particular sector. The industry was the first to recognize that change is necessary and, as partners with the supply management system, we in government must do the same. We must recognize that there are difficulties, but we must also be prepared to make changes.
In the area of safety net programs, for instance, the Farm Income Protection Act was brought in to really emphasize the whole farm approach to agriculture and to increase this co-operation, this tripartite agreement and the aspect of the agricultural farm community supporting one another in an income support program. That seems to make a lot more sense than some of the ad hoc programs that seem to have happened in the past. This seems to be an ongoing thing where people are contributing from within the industry, that they are not just waiting for a handout.
Certainly the farmers in my community whom I have spoken to are very pleased with this. It has got some problems and I will be the first one to tell you that, but they are very pleased with the concept and getting themselves involved with it. That becomes very healthy in that particular aspect of it.
When you look at this program, the Farm Income Protection Act, it has four parts that are really very critical to it, the Net Income Stabilization Account which I have talked about, the Gross Revenue Insurance Program, and a crop insurance program. Those are the kinds of things that farmers are looking for to really get things under way and to make their industry competitive in the 1990s and beyond in the next century.
I think there is co-operation of governments at various levels, and co-operation of consumers who certainly are the end user. They have a very strong vested interest in this particular situation and it is very important that they do that.
November 8, 1991

The act also sets out very important principles for the establishment of any new program. The program should not unduly influence producer production and marketing decisions. The level of protection provided should be reasonably consistent with all other agreements, taking into account regional diversity.
The programs should be compatible with our international obligations. One more point, the program should encourage long-term environmental and economic sustainability. To this end we have recently announced the special assistance program of over $800 million. There have been other committees to examine special needs, whether it be oilseeds or sugar beets.
It is evident that we have in place a policy that will provide short and long term protection to the family farm to ensure that income gaps within the farming community are addressed.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity this afternoon to speak to the motion of the hon. member from Saskatchewan concerning the difficulties facing agriculture today, especially the need for marketing boards, income plans, price guarantees, and other arrangements to make agriculture in this country and in other countries viable.
I do not suppose there has been a time in recent history where there was a greater concern or financial uncertainty or uncertainty about the future than there is this fall. Certainly there has never been a time in Canadian history when so much was being decided in Geneva, Switzerland, that would have such a profound impact on Canadian farmers.
For the last six years the United States through its export enhancement program and other arrangements has been engaged in a price war to try to bludgeon the European Economic Community into submission and to try to regain part of the eastern European market for grain that it lost after the embargo which it placed on grain to Russia at the time of the Afghanistan war in 1980.
To try to achieve this it is spending something between $900 million and $1.2 billion subsidizing wheat and grain that would normally sell on the market for $135 or $150 a tonne for anywhere between $50 a tonne to $75 a tonne. It does not take a very wise person to realize that if farmers are getting something like $75 a tonne, or $2 a bushel for grain that costs them $4 or $5 a bushel to
Private Members' Business
produce, grain that has not sold for those prices since the early 1960s, there is absolute total chaos in the grain producing areas of our country, especially the prairie provinces. It extends of course to the grains and oilseeds sector of Ontario and other provinces as well.
At the same time that we face that kind of chaos in world markets for grains and oilseeds, the supply management sector of Canadian agriculture, that is the dairy sector and the poultry sector are absolutely petrified that this government is going to sell them out in the negotiations there and adopt an American proposal called tariffication which essentially would have a devastating impact on that sector of our agricultural economy which is the most stable, which is the most self-reliant, where people pay for their food in the grocery store rather than have it paid for from the public purse.
Thrown into this mix of uncertainty, last year because of the accelerated subsidies by the United States and by the European community countries, world prices for grain dropped from something close to $4 a bushel to about $2 a bushel. At the same time that was happening during the summer, fall and winter months of 1990, the Government of Canada in its wisdom chopped government support programs by almost 40 per cent. It chopped them from roughly $3.2 billion to $1.9 billion in that crop year.
It is not hard to understand why farmers are protesting across this country in little communities like Lucknow, where over 1,000 people showed up at a rally in early September, and in a half dozen other communities across Canada, including the largest one which was held just a couple of weeks ago in Regina where over 7,000 farmers showed up to protest the government's cutting of support programs by $1.3 billion, a 40 per cent reduction at a time when world prices were dropping by 30 per cent. Never has there been greater uncertainty for Canadian agriculture. That is a pity because Canadian agriculture is efficient. It is talented. It has a good resource base. It should be productive. It is very productive, but it should be reasonably profitable.
We have Canadian farmers today who have an average investment of over half a million dollars, $500,000 average, whose average income in 1989, which was a good year and it might be even lower today, was about $17,000. That is less than what the average farm family earns off the farm where the spouse has a job in the community.

November 8, 1991
Private Members' Business
As this motion proposes, it is absolutely essential that we try to bring order out of chaos. We need to have orderly marketing. We need to maintain the orderly marketing we have. If the government sells out the dairymen and the poultrymen, you are going to have that sector of our agricultural economy which has been the most stable, the most reliable, the most self-reliant, lined up at the steps of the legislature and lined up at the steps of Parliament, demanding billions of dollars of compensation, stabilization and support programs. So it is absolutely essential that the government maintain that orderly marketing in the domestic scene.
I hope from these GATT negotiations likewise that there will be an orderly marketing arrangement devised at the international level.
In 1968 we had an international grains agreement which proposed an arrangement among the producing countries of the world to share the market in a fair and equitable way. Attached to that was a food stabilization accord or agreement. I think that regardless of what happens at the GATT, we should have an international food fund. We have an International Monetary Fund to try to bring some stability and order out of the situation that we have in monetary and economic affairs of the world. We should have an international food fund as well, in my opinion.
We are spending about $300 billion to subsidize food around the world. For countries that have no other means of feeding their peoples, that is great. Flowever, we have the insane situation where we are subsidizing everybody. Canadian farmers earn about four cents on a loaf of bread that costs $1.29 in a grocery store.
It does not take much imagination to realize why there is so much chaos. What I feel we should be doing is putting some part of this $300 billion that we are spending to subsidize into an international food fund which would provide assistance and support to those nations and peoples of the world who cannot afford to feed themselves. It would assist them in providing food.
We should let the rest of the world that can afford the proper price that gives the producer a reasonable return
provide it. Let the market work. Let the people who can afford to pay an adequate price for their food pay for it.
If we want to solve the international farm financial crisis we must have orderly marketing internationally and domestically. That is not to say that every commodity will have supply management like we have for poultry and dairy.
Clearly for commodities marketed internationally to a great per cent it is not very practical to have a supply management system like we have for dairy and poultry in this country. There has to be reasonable, fair rules so countries like Canada that have a natural advantage in grains and oilseeds can sell them on the world market. We sell about 80 per cent on the world market in a fair and equitable way.
We might have to lower our input costs to be competitive with the United States and some other countries, but clearly the motion today talks about orderly marketing both nationally and internationally. These are my ideas of what this government and what governments around the world need to do if as a nation we are to provide a reasonable, sane, sensible way of maintaining our agricultural community and giving a reasonable return to those producers who work so hard, have such a massive capital investment and deserve a better situation than they have in Canada or around the world today.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in the debate this afternoon in response to the motion put forward by the member for Mackenzie.
If we look at some of the recent statistics in this country we can understand why the member for Mackenzie and others from western Canada are concerned about what is happening in agriculture. One of the things I wanted to do to reinforce that concern was to point out an article in The Globe and Mail today at which I am sure the hon. member for Mackenzie and most likely the member for Algoma have had a chance to take a look. The Canadian Press articles mentions Saskatchewan specifically and the outpouring of people from that province. It tells us that the province of Saskatchewan lost 19,442 more people to other parts of the country than what it gained in return in the latest statistics available. That is a rate of something in the order of 19.3

November 8, 1991

per cent of its residents in the last couple of years. I believe that statistic is based on the 1989-90 year.
Those are very alarming statistics. It is not the only agricultural province that is registering those kinds of numbers. It is happening in other provinces as well, but most of them are coming from the farm. The farm sector is certainly under siege. There is no question about it. As the member for Algoma mentioned, we are into a subsidy war and Canada is paying a big price for that.
The price tag on that subsidy war between the United States and the European countries alone is running in the neighbourhood of $300 billion at an annual rate. There appears to be no end in sight. The treasuries of the United States and European countries apparently can afford to play that game although I am not convinced they can afford to play it. For the last number of years they have been content to play that game without coming to grips with the real problem. I think we are in full agreement with that.
The consumer at the end of the day pays the price for a commodity whether it is through taxes or at the checkout counter at the grocery store. To assume that Canada could take part in that high stakes game is an unreal perspective. We cannot and we do not want the Europeans and Americans to continue along that course. It is a very destructive course and we certainly pay the price in this country.
The statistics I mentioned in relation to the numbers of people leaving farms in western Canada and other parts of Canada tell the real story. If you are getting $2 a bushel for wheat there is no way you can pay the bills at the end of the day. We have to find a way to get out from under that.
Both of the members on the opposition side mentioned a couple of commodities. It is interesting that they did and I do want to reflect on what they said. The member for Mackenzie mentioned the price of beer in relation to the price of barley. As we all know in the beer process, barley is one of the key ingredients that has to be used in the production of that commodity. Obviously the grain farmer is not reaping the reward for his work
Private Members' Business
and for the product they use to manufacture the end product which is beer.
How can we achieve something different? The same is in relation to the price of bread. They are saying that a farmer gets about 4 cents for his grain when it is all factored into the price of that loaf of bread.
I do not have the answer to it but the trend today is vertical integration in the marketplace. Maybe that is an area we have to move more into in this country. Obviously there is risk in doing that because vertical integration means bigger companies and bigger farms with more assets than we would like to see in the hands of one group. The reason is that it probably means the end of the family farm if one competes on that level. I am not saying it is the answer but it is certainly a reality in other parts of our industrial society.
There was a conference sponsored by The Financial Post in Toronto yesterday. Some of the big players were there to take part in it and to take a look at this world-wide phenomenon of size in relation to marketing and products manufactured and how at the end of the day they can survive out there in the marketplace.
They were talking about the European market, for example. That is dominated by a handful of companies really. It is companies like Nestle, Unilever, Phillip Morris and BSN. They actually take a look at McCain Foods as well and some of the success they enjoy in Europe. They are big companies. To compete and to work through that whole chain where the consumer picks their product up at the supermarket, you have to have that integration within your industiy to be able to do that. At the end of the day one must have the price that will attract the consumer to buy one's product.
It is not all big business in my province of New Brunswick but one of the things we have been able to do is have the value added to some of those products in our province. Take the example of just selling the raw material. By selling grains like wheat and barley there is not a whole lot of profit there. Maybe that is something that some of the western provinces might take a look at.
For example, in New Brunswick the figure to value add it on our product is something in the order of 40 to 50 per cent. It is one of the highest in the nation. Whereas if we go into Saskatchewan I think that figure is in the 3 or 4 per cent range. Maybe the answer lies in vertical integration, taking value and putting the value on those prod-

ucts and further processing of those products before they leave the province.
If you want to take a look at the beer industry, Madam Speaker, that is a unique one. As you know at the end of the day you are talking about a very high priced product. I think there is probably an opportunity there for western grain fanners to take a look at how that product is used in the end product and maybe some improvements can be made in that process in western Canada.
Why is it that at the end of the day the key ingredient in that product, the barley, is a very small percentage of the price at the supermarket or the liquor store? It is the same with a loaf of bread or a box of cornflakes, as the members here have pointed out so often. I think the price of a box of cornflakes is less than 10 per cent of the price of the product. There certainly is room for improvement.
The motion before us reads:
That, in the opinion of the House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing marketing boards, income plans and price guarantees to ensure the income gaps within the farming community are narrowed and to ensure a continued supply of quality foodstuffs at reasonable and stable prices.
Not one of us here is going to disagree with that statement. But how do we achieve that is the question.
I see that my time is quickly running out, but I want to reinforce the government's commitment to supply management. The minister is on record today during Question Period as stating that our commitment is an ongoing commitment. We have not waffled in regard to that. We
are going to continue with clarification of article XI. We are not going to give up on it. We are not going to cave in to international pressures.
There is a great deal at stake in the farming community and we realize that. We are going to continue to pursue the strengthening and clarification of article XI. At the same time we do have a task force out there examining milk marketing boards in attempt to identify what can be done within those marketing boards to improve efficiency and return for farmers within those marketing board structures.
It is a two-way street. I believe that our marketing board people are doing their best with those marketing board commodities that relate to the agricultural sector, but the government of the day is also doing its job. We are defending it and will continue to defend it. We will do it in the best interest of all of us: the consumer and the farmer.
